regions.name: The instrument
regions.blurb: Premise P1. Does a firing neuron measure a meme? Reliability and validity of the unit itself.
regions.state: Four small tests run, all mixed. No unit has been shown to follow an idea across rewording at scale, and there is no human check and no steering. Everything else rests on this.

regions.name: Across models
regions.blurb: Premise P2. Do different models, languages and media give the same reading?
regions.state: Twins across models turned out to be mostly shared word detectors. No learned map, no held-out text and no second language has been tried.

regions.name: The atlas
regions.blurb: A catalogue of the units: a reference list, a periodic table of memes, and the mechanism behind them.
regions.state: Batman's name-free core turned out to be the textbook definition of a superhero. No catalogue of validated units exists yet.

regions.name: Old memetics, re-run
regions.blurb: Claims from Dawkins-era and internet memetics that never had a unit.
regions.state: Untouched. Internet-meme studies have public data and published results to re-derive. All of them were done with words.

regions.name: Lineage
regions.blurb: Who descends from whom, including influence nobody declared.
regions.state: The one robust result lives here: heredity. Word counts find it too, and trees built from memes failed. It needs lineages where the wording changes.

regions.name: Remix and influence
regions.blurb: How much of a work is inherited, how much is new, and who influenced whom.
regions.state: Nothing run. Similarity is not influence, so only cases where influence is documented can test it.

regions.name: Population memetics
regions.blurb: Drift, selection, linkage and flow of memes across whole populations of works.
regions.state: Only descriptive timelines so far. Several statistics can be computed from data already committed.

regions.name: Cultural evolution, re-run
regions.blurb: The accepted science of cultural change, tested with the new unit.
regions.state: Untouched. Decades of predictions about what survives retelling, with public data, waiting for a unit.

regions.name: Fitness and forecasting
regions.blurb: Which memes and combinations succeed, and whether that can be predicted.
regions.state: One underpowered test, no signal. Content explains little of success unless author and timing are held fixed. Archives of randomised headline tests fix that.

regions.name: Meme engineering
regions.blurb: Turning a meme up or down in a text, and breeding better variants.
regions.state: Nothing run. Steering is the missing causal test, and plain prompting is the rival to beat.

regions.name: Field conjectures
regions.blurb: Hunches from marketing practice, made testable.
regions.state: About 35 hunches from practice, none measured.

regions.name: Uses
regions.blurb: What the instrument is good for outside the lab.
regions.state: Nothing run in the open. Any score built on these units first has to survive attempts to game it with trigger words.

ideas.title: Is there a canon beyond chance?
ideas.question: Do neuron units pick out a core that random sets of films lack?
ideas.result: Yes. No random 32-film set has a single neuron present in 23 or more of its films; Batman has 1,534 (Qwen3-8B). Names were present, so much of this core is name detectors.
ideas.method: 50 random 32-film pseudo-franchises against the 32 Batman works.
ideas.rivals: None run for this count.
ideas.premise: P1: the unit is countable and repeatable. It does not show the unit is a concept.
ideas.bio: Core genome of a species

ideas.title: Blind test of the meme labels
ideas.question: Can a blind judge match a neuron's label to a new sentence it fires on?
ideas.result: 56 of 71 right (79%). A judge that only compares word stems gets 65%. For the 31 showcase memes the gap is not significant (77% against 63%, p = 0.07). Judges were AI; item-level answers were not kept.
ideas.method: Two-choice test on held-out sentences.
ideas.rivals: Word-stem overlap judge.
ideas.premise: P1: labels carry some meaning beyond chance, little beyond words.
ideas.bio: Checking a gene annotation

ideas.title: Ideas or words: the rewording test
ideas.question: Does a unit still fire when its top sentence is rewritten with no shared content words?
ideas.result: 11 of 31 Qwen units passed a lenient bar (5.0 expected by chance). Only 2 Qwen units and 6 Llama units were specific to their own rewording. Every Qwen character unit but one failed without the name.
ideas.method: 31 rewritten sentences, scored against ten everyday sentences and a mismatched-rewording null.
ideas.rivals: Mismatched rewording.
ideas.premise: P1: a few units track ideas; most track words.
ideas.bio: Synonymous substitutions

ideas.title: One concept unit: revenge
ideas.question: Is there a neuron for revenge that works without revenge words?
ideas.result: Llama's unit chose the revenge sentence in 10 of 12 new minimal pairs. Qwen's unit, picked the same way, scored 4 of 12: it was a keyword detector. The two units correlate at only 0.39.
ideas.method: Unit chosen on 10 practice pairs, scored on 12 new pairs with no revenge words.
ideas.rivals: The keyword itself.
ideas.premise: P1: possible for some concepts in some models. P2: the two models did not agree.
ideas.bio: A single well-characterised gene

ideas.title: Twins across two companies' models
ideas.question: Does each Qwen meme have a matching neuron in Llama?
ideas.result: The 33 strongest have twins at median r = 0.82, but equally word-like non-meme units reach 0.86. Across all 14,843 families the median is 0.40 against 0.36 for random units. Without names the same pairs fall to 0.14.
ideas.method: Best-correlated Llama unit over 3,700 sentences, with nulls matched on sparsity, layer and word-likeness.
ideas.rivals: Word-matched non-meme units.
ideas.premise: P2: name and word detectors recur. Concept units recur weakly.
ideas.bio: Orthologous genes

ideas.title: Do two models draw the same tree?
ideas.question: Do Qwen and Llama agree on which works carry which memes and how works relate?
ideas.result: Distance matrices correlate at 0.98, but random units give 0.90 to 0.93 and two word methods agree at 0.92. Presence grids agree at kappa 0.73 against 0.35 to 0.57 for controls.
ideas.method: Mantel correlation and Cohen's kappa, with random-unit and TF-IDF floors.
ideas.rivals: Random units; TF-IDF against LSA.
ideas.premise: P2: agreement is mostly a floor any text representation reaches, with a small excess.
ideas.bio: Gene trees agreeing across loci

ideas.title: A smaller sibling model
ideas.question: Does Qwen3-1.7B, from the same family, agree better than a different company's model?
ideas.result: No. Median twin r is 0.40, the same as for Llama. The agreement level seems to reflect the text more than shared training. Never run on name-free texts.
ideas.method: Same pipeline on Qwen3-1.7B.
ideas.rivals: Random active units (0.36).
ideas.premise: P2: no extra convergence within a model family.
ideas.bio: Sister species

ideas.title: Vision neurons on posters
ideas.question: Do image-model neurons find Batman memes in posters and covers?
ideas.result: Exploratory. CLIP has 56 neurons present in 6 or more of 29 Batman images against 0.6 by chance. No cheap rival was compared and it is not part of the paper.
ideas.method: CLIP RN50x4 and DINOv2 neurons on one image per work.
ideas.rivals: None.
ideas.premise: P2 across media: untested in any strict sense.
ideas.bio: The same gene in another tissue

ideas.title: Family trees from meme sets
ideas.question: Does a tree built from shared memes put each adaptation next to its source comic?
ideas.result: No. The source ranks 5.4 of 12 by tree distance against 5.8 by chance. Word counts put it at 2.9, and random non-meme units beat the selected memes in every draw.
ideas.method: Jaccard distance on meme sets, neighbour joining.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF, LSA, random units. All won.
ideas.premise: P1: the selected 'memes' were worse than unselected units, so the selection rule is suspect.
ideas.bio: Phylogenetic tree inference

ideas.title: Heredity: adaptations carry their sources
ideas.question: With every name removed, do adaptations carry their documented source comic's optional units more than other comics'?
ideas.result: Yes, in both models: 16% and 10% of comics beat the source against 47% by chance (exact p = 0.0026 and 0.00017), in 99.6% of 30,240 analysis variants. Word counts do as well (11%).
ideas.method: Pre-registered E2: 9 adaptations, 12 comics, exact permutation test.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF cosine and word presence. They matched the neurons.
ideas.premise: Shows heredity is measurable in these texts. Does not show neurons are needed.
ideas.bio: Parentage testing

ideas.title: Do neurons add anything beyond shared words?
ideas.question: After word similarity is regressed out, does neuron inheritance still point to the source?
ideas.result: Not for Qwen (p = 0.09 to 0.25). Marginally for Llama (p = 0.010 to 0.033), but that falls to 0.057 to 0.065 under the stricter nulls and is uncorrected for six tests. Word counts keep their signal with neurons removed.
ideas.method: Pre-registered residual test over 32 by 12 pairs.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and word presence.
ideas.premise: The key test of P1's added value. Failed on the primary model.
ideas.bio: Signal left after controlling for population structure

ideas.title: The vigilante lineage
ideas.question: Do the Scarlet Pimpernel, Zorro, Batman and Iron Man show up as one family?
ideas.result: Partly. They share the superhero layer (the secret identity) and not Batman's own trappings. One summary each, names present, Zorro only 9 sentences: inconclusive.
ideas.method: Nearest relatives and six orphan-vigilante memes across 13 relatives.
ideas.rivals: None.
ideas.premise: Illustrative only.
ideas.bio: Deep homology

ideas.title: Identity: what makes a story Batman?
ideas.question: Without names, does the share of Batman's canon a work carries separate Batman from other masked heroes?
ideas.result: No: AUC 0.52 and 0.54 against 8 hero films, where a word-based score gets 0.80 and text length alone 0.76. It does separate Batman from ordinary films (0.90 to 0.95).
ideas.method: Pre-registered E1, held-out works, name-free texts.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF centroid and text length. Both won.
ideas.premise: P1: the canon-share score missed what words caught.
ideas.bio: Species diagnosis

ideas.title: The name-free core is the superhero template
ideas.question: What is left of Batman's core when names are removed?
ideas.result: Seven Qwen units: a secret identity, an origin in loss, a costume, a mission by night. They are present in 91% of the hero films too. The neurons rediscovered the standard definition of a superhero. Descriptive, not a test.
ideas.method: Units present in at least 70% of name-free Batman works.
ideas.rivals: None.
ideas.premise: Suggestive for P1: the surviving units are concept-like.
ideas.bio: Conserved genes of a genus

ideas.title: Selection: do popular works' memes spread?
ideas.question: Do memes carried by popular early works spread further into later works?
ideas.result: No signal: rho = 0.25 (p = 0.35) and 0.00 (p = 0.58). The test had 15 works and would catch a true correlation of 0.3 only 27% of the time. A weak null.
ideas.method: Pre-registered E3: pageviews against residualised spread.
ideas.rivals: Reverse-time placebo.
ideas.premise: Says nothing about P1 or P2. Selection needs a bigger lineage and success measured at release.
ideas.bio: Detecting selection

ideas.title: When memes enter and where they recur
ideas.question: Can each meme's first appearance and later spread be placed on a timeline?
ideas.result: Yes, descriptively. But 6 of 15 optional memes 'first appear' in 1986 only because the sample has no works from 1967 to 1985.
ideas.method: First appearance of each named meme among the 32 works.
ideas.rivals: None.
ideas.premise: Shows the bookkeeping works. The sample is too thin for any claim.
ideas.bio: Dating a gene's origin

ideas.title: Planted memes: neurons against keywords
ideas.question: When a meme is written into a story without its usual words, do neurons detect it better than a keyword analyst or a word classifier?
ideas.hypothesis: H1 of the pre-registration: neurons beat both word rivals by at least 0.05 AUC on reworded stories.
ideas.falsifier: The gap is credibly below 0.05 AUC against either rival.
ideas.data: 816 stories to be written (136 plots in 6 versions), 3 of 34 memes planted in each. Truth is known by construction.
ideas.method: Each planted story against its own control version, per meme.
ideas.rivals: Evasion-aware keyword lists and TF-IDF logistic regression.
ideas.premise: P1. The cleanest planned test of whether neurons see ideas when words change.
ideas.bio: Spike-in controls
ideas.cost: L: about 4,400 agent sessions and 3 days as designed; a trimmed version takes 1.5 days
ideas.risk: Power is only 0.22 to 0.40 at the smallest effect of interest, and every story, reader and rater is one AI model family.

ideas.title: Planted memes: neurons against embeddings
ideas.question: Are neurons at least as good as the strongest sentence embeddings at finding a planted meme?
ideas.hypothesis: H2: neurons are within 0.05 AUC of Qwen3-Embedding-4B and e5-large.
ideas.falsifier: Neurons are credibly worse than any one of the three embedding rivals by more than 0.05.
ideas.data: The same 816 planted stories.
ideas.method: Non-inferiority test, then superiority.
ideas.rivals: Qwen3-Embedding-4B on sentences and on 3-sentence windows; e5-large.
ideas.premise: P1. If embeddings win, the case for neurons rests on being nameable and cheap, not on accuracy.
ideas.bio: Comparing two sequencing platforms
ideas.cost: L: shares the planted-story run
ideas.risk: Power 0.22 when the two are truly equal.

ideas.title: Do Batman's concept units travel to other genres?
ideas.question: Do the 11 concept units found on Batman texts respond to their own meme, and only that meme, in unrelated stories?
ideas.hypothesis: H3: each unit's detection of its own meme exceeds its detection of other memes by at least 0.05 AUC.
ideas.falsifier: Specificity credibly below 0.05: the units fire on any eventful passage.
ideas.data: The planted stories, in genres far from Batman.
ideas.method: Own-meme AUC minus other-meme AUC, labels permuted across units.
ideas.rivals: Label permutation; the same test for word and name units.
ideas.premise: P1. Tests whether a unit found in one corpus is a portable concept.
ideas.bio: Does a gene do the same job in another species
ideas.cost: L: shares the planted-story run
ideas.risk: Power 0.14 at the smallest effect of interest.

ideas.title: Is one neuron enough?
ideas.question: Does a single neuron detect a meme as well as five, and does the neuron basis beat the same model's dense hidden states?
ideas.hypothesis: 'Single neurons are memes' is claimed only if five neurons beat one by less than 0.03 AUC.
ideas.falsifier: Five neurons, or the pooled hidden state, clearly beat one neuron.
ideas.data: The planted stories.
ideas.method: One unit against five; neurons against hidden states at four layers.
ideas.rivals: The model's own hidden states.
ideas.premise: P1. Asks whether the neuron is the right unit or just one readout of a dense representation.
ideas.bio: One gene or a polygenic trait
ideas.cost: L: shares the planted-story run

ideas.title: Are neurons easier to name than topics?
ideas.question: Can blind judges match labels to neurons better than to LDA topics or embedding clusters?
ideas.hypothesis: Neuron labels beat a word-overlap floor and are at least as nameable as topics and clusters.
ideas.falsifier: Topics or clusters are as nameable; neurons do not beat the word floor.
ideas.data: Labels written for units, topics and clusters on the planted stories.
ideas.method: Blind two-choice label test, 12 tests.
ideas.rivals: LDA topics, embedding clusters, word-overlap judge.
ideas.premise: P1: nameability is the one advantage claimed for neurons over embeddings.
ideas.bio: Annotating genes against annotating markers
ideas.cost: M: about 1,300 agent sessions; first candidate to cut

ideas.title: Natural summaries annotated by hand
ideas.question: On real plot summaries labelled exhaustively for memes, which method agrees best with the annotators?
ideas.hypothesis: Neurons match annotators at least as well as keywords and embeddings.
ideas.falsifier: They trail both.
ideas.data: 237 name-masked natural summaries, to be annotated.
ideas.method: Two annotators plus an adjudicator; each method scored against them.
ideas.rivals: Keywords, embeddings, LLM reading.
ideas.premise: P1 on natural text.
ideas.bio: Curated reference annotations
ideas.cost: M: about 600 agent sessions. Deferred
ideas.risk: AI annotators recognise masked works and label from memory. Needs human annotators to mean much.

ideas.title: Heredity across languages
ideas.question: Do neurons still find the source comic when the adaptation's summary is in Chinese and the comic's is in English?
ideas.hypothesis: Neurons recover sources across languages where word overlap cannot.
ideas.falsifier: Neurons fall to chance, or trail multilingual embeddings and machine translation plus word counts.
ideas.data: The Batman lineage translated into Simplified Chinese; a natural zh.wikipedia arm.
ideas.method: The E2 statistic across languages.
ideas.rivals: Machine translation plus TF-IDF; multilingual embeddings.
ideas.premise: Both. Shared wording cannot carry the signal, so a pass would be the first clear win over words.
ideas.bio: The same gene in a different genome
ideas.cost: M: about 850 agent sessions. Deferred
ideas.risk: Chinese is not a supported Llama 3.1 language; translators may bring back the canonical names.

ideas.title: Concept agreement on held-out films
ideas.question: Do 27 Qwen concept units have Llama partners that agree on 1,000 unseen random films better than word-matched control units?
ideas.hypothesis: Concept units agree across models more than 81 lexically matched null units.
ideas.falsifier: No advantage over the word-matched nulls on held-out text.
ideas.data: 1,000 random film summaries already collected (preregistration/sources/t3_random_films.jsonl.gz).
ideas.method: Twins fixed on development text, scored on held-out films.
ideas.rivals: Lexically matched non-meme units.
ideas.premise: P2. The first out-of-sample test of cross-model agreement. Data is already in hand.
ideas.bio: Orthologues confirmed in new samples
ideas.cost: S: extraction on 1,000 summaries. Deferred

ideas.title: The vocabulary drift ladder
ideas.question: As more of an adaptation's content words are replaced, how long does each method still find its source?
ideas.hypothesis: H4: neurons keep finding the source at 50 to 100% replacement where TF-IDF and LSA lose it.
ideas.falsifier: Neurons degrade as fast as word counts.
ideas.data: Batman and Shakespeare-film summaries rewritten at 25, 50, 75 and 100% replacement, with a style-only control.
ideas.method: Source recovery at each level.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF, LSA. Embeddings and an LLM reader should be added.
ideas.premise: P1. A lineage where wording changes and ideas stay is exactly what the paper says is needed.
ideas.bio: Tracing descent through synonymous change
ideas.cost: M: about 850 agent sessions. Deferred
ideas.risk: Power 0.15 at the smallest effect of interest; the rewriter may leak source words.

ideas.title: Shakespeare: a fresh lineage
ideas.question: Do loose film adaptations of Shakespeare carry their play's memes when names, settings and wording all differ?
ideas.hypothesis: H5: neurons rank the true play above other plays for renamed adaptations.
ideas.falsifier: No better than chance, or no better than words.
ideas.data: 40 plays and 54 films of 13 plays with documented sources (preregistration/works_shakespeare.json).
ideas.method: E2-style source recovery.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF, LSA.
ideas.premise: P1 on a second lineage.
ideas.bio: A second model organism
ideas.cost: M. Deferred
ideas.risk: Ground truth is weaker than it looks: 27 of 83 loose films rested on a Wikipedia category; Romeo and Juliet dominates. Power 0.17.

ideas.title: Batman-likeness across 2,544 works
ideas.question: Scored on Batman's own units, do documented Batman relatives rank above a large pool of other works?
ideas.hypothesis: Documented relatives (Zorro, the Pimpernel, Iron Man and others) rank above the pool.
ideas.falsifier: They do not, or TF-IDF, LSA and embeddings rank them as well.
ideas.data: 2,544 name-masked works, 62,879 sentences, with 36 documented relatives (preregistration/culture_pool.json).
ideas.method: Rank relatives against the pool.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF, LSA, embeddings, an LLM 'likeness' judge.
ideas.premise: Uses both. Finds the other billionaire vigilante orphans in the culture.
ideas.bio: Homology search across a database
ideas.cost: M. Deferred
ideas.risk: Franchises are not independent works; earlier drafts had Batman stories among the negatives.

ideas.title: Mutation and selection against a neutral model
ideas.question: Are units that first appear in landmark works carried forward more than random copying predicts?
ideas.hypothesis: Units new in The Dark Knight Returns, Year One and The Killing Joke spread more than a margin-preserving null allows.
ideas.falsifier: Spread is no greater than the neutral model's.
ideas.data: 71 Batman works (32 development, 39 test).
ideas.method: New units per work, tested against a neutral random-copying model.
ideas.rivals: The same test on words.
ideas.premise: Uses both. The first population-level test.
ideas.bio: Selection against neutral drift
ideas.cost: M. Deferred
ideas.risk: Circular: the added works include direct adaptations of the predicted innovators, and 42 of 43 new works are from 1995 on.

ideas.title: Cost against accuracy, head to head
ideas.question: Is any rival method both at least as accurate as neurons and no more expensive per story?
ideas.hypothesis: H6: no rival dominates.
ideas.falsifier: Any rival is at least as accurate and no dearer.
ideas.data: The planted stories; timings already measured.
ideas.method: Cost per story at 34 memes against accuracy, 17 methods.
ideas.rivals: Keywords, embeddings, topics, LLM judges, NLI.
ideas.premise: Practical value. One neuron pass costs about as much as one uncached LLM yes-or-no question.
ideas.bio: Sequencing cost per genome
ideas.cost: L: shares the planted-story run

ideas.title: Catching coded language
ideas.question: When a group renames an idea with an invented code word, do methods that read context still find it?
ideas.hypothesis: Neurons, hidden states and an LLM judge beat sentence embeddings and keyword lists on code-word versions.
ideas.falsifier: Context-free methods do as well.
ideas.data: Code-word versions of the planted stories.
ideas.method: Six tests on Qwen; the headline is stated only if all six pass.
ideas.rivals: Evasion-aware keywords, sentence embeddings.
ideas.premise: P1, and a use: moderation when vocabulary is changed to evade filters.
ideas.bio: Detecting a gene under a different name
ideas.cost: L: shares the planted-story run
ideas.risk: Invented code words are not real evasive language. No real-world corpus is in the plan.

ideas.title: Minimal pairs and decoys for thirty story concepts
ideas.question: For how many story concepts does a neuron chosen on development pairs respond to the concept, and not to its words or to any dramatic event, on held-out pairs?
ideas.hypothesis: In Qwen3-8B, the primary model, at least 15 of 30 concepts have a frozen unit that ranks the concept sentence above its matched control in 16 or more of 20 held-out pairs. Pooled over concepts, AUC (chance 0.5) is at least 0.80 on concept-without-its-words against words-without-the-concept. Llama 3.1 8B is reported as a replication.
ideas.falsifier: Fewer than 8 of 30 concepts reach 16 of 20; or units picked on shuffled development labels pass as often; or a unit wins as often on other concepts' pairs as on its own; or pooled mixed-cell AUC is under 0.70. Separately, a margin under 0.05 over the best embedding detector means the units add inspectability only.
ideas.data: Built by construction: 30 concepts with near neighbours (revenge, vow, harm). Per concept 60 minimal pairs (the concept told without its usual words; the same frame with another event of equal stakes) and 40 decoys using the words without the concept; 4,800 sentences. Written by an untested model family; 300 hand-checked. CC BY 4.0. 40 pairs development, 20 test.
ideas.method: Units: neuron poles (one sign of one MLP neuron) in Qwen3-8B, Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3-1.7B. Shortlist 20 per concept on half the development pairs, pick one on the rest, hash before test items exist. Score held-out pair wins and pooled mixed-cell AUC; bootstrap over concepts. Nulls: shuffled-label selection, other concepts' pairs, word-matched units. Chance of 16 of 20: 0.006.
ideas.rivals: Keyword list and TF-IDF (fail by construction), sentence-embedding prototype, zero-shot LLM reader from a third model family, mean-pooled residual stream probe, sentence length. Most dangerous: the LLM reader, likely near ceiling. If it wins we still learn what share of concepts have a word-independent unit, which the study measured for one concept only.
ideas.premise: P1. A pass shows concept units exist beyond one hand-picked case. A fail on most concepts, after Qwen's revenge unit scored 4 of 12 (study/results/wording.json), would mean neurons in 8B models mostly read words.
ideas.bio: Knock-in with a matched control: change one thing, read one output
ideas.cost: S to M. About 4,800 short sentences, three extraction passes of minutes each, a few dollars of writing and reading calls; 3 to 5 days, mostly checking items.
ideas.payoff: A count of validated concept units per model, with the drop from development to test, and a frozen unit list that later designs and the steering area can reuse.
ideas.risk: LLM-written pairs carry a style cue, so units or embeddings may win on style. Sentences are read alone, while the study read whole documents, so units that need long context may be missed.
ideas.review: Raised development pairs from 20 to 40 with a two-stage pick: with 20, about one of 884,736 units wins every pair by chance. Added a cross-concept null, a primary model and a pooled AUC. It is the cheap sentence-level cousin of the unrun planted-story plan. Style cues remain.

ideas.title: Are 8B 4-bit neurons cleaner than random directions?
ideas.question: Do neuron poles in the study's quantised 8B models pass a blind coherence test more often than random directions, and can the test see planted mixtures?
ideas.hypothesis: In an odd-one-out test (two sentences from a unit's strongest examples plus one from another unit; chance 33%), accuracy is at least 20 points higher for neuron poles than for random directions in the same layers, and planted two-neuron mixtures score at least 15 points below single neurons.
ideas.falsifier: Neuron minus random-direction gap under 10 points; or mixtures within 5 points of single neurons (the test cannot see mixing, so no cleanliness claim is possible); or a word-overlap picker matches the blind grader on neuron items (coherent only as word detectors); or a weight-shuffled model scores within 10 points of the trained one.
ideas.data: FineWeb sample, about 10 million tokens of web text (ODC-By), for activations; no labels needed. Per model: 300 random poles stratified by layer third, 300 random unit-norm directions in the same MLP hidden spaces, 150 sums of two unrelated poles, each scaled to its own maximum. Models: Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B, 4-bit MLX builds.
ideas.method: Per unit, 6 triplets from its 20 strongest sentences, peak token marked, odd sentence length-matched. A two-job mixture then has no right answer half the time, so mixing shows. Blind grader: an LLM from another family; a human does 200 items. Accuracy by unit type and layer third, bootstrapped; 300 per arm puts 10 points at 4 standard errors.
ideas.rivals: A word-overlap picker (choose the sentence least similar by TF-IDF) and an embedding picker on the same items; random directions; the weight-shuffled model. Most dangerous: the word-overlap picker. If it matches the grader, the neurons are coherent only as word detectors, which is still the answer P1 needs.
ideas.premise: P1. A clear gap on these exact models licenses their neurons as units. No gap, or a test blind to mixtures, removes the source essay's support for the study's models.
ideas.bio: Mock community of known composition, with positive and negative controls
ideas.cost: M. One extraction pass of about two hours per model plus one for the shuffled model, about 9,000 grader calls (modest API spend or a local 9B model), 3 hours of human checking; about a week.
ideas.payoff: The first cleanliness figure for 8B 4-bit models, by layer, with a noise floor and a sensitivity check that the source essay lacked and its outside retest failed.
ideas.risk: Coherence is not concept detection: name and token detectors pass. Ten million tokens may not reach many neurons' strong regime, so the 20 strongest sentences are partly weak firings.
ideas.review: Replaced the five-way intruder test: with four unit sentences a two-job mixture still has an obvious odd one out, so the mixture control could not fail. Triplets fix that. The word-overlap picker is now a falsifier. Remaining: an LLM grader, and coherence rewards word detectors.

ideas.title: Presence by the neuron's own strong regime
ideas.question: Are the study's presence calls made in each unit's strong regime, and do the units' labels hold only there?
ideas.hypothesis: At least 30% of presence calls for the 125 labelled units fall below 30% of the unit's own maximum, and blind label-matching accuracy is at least 15 points lower for sentences at 5 to 20% of maximum than for sentences above 50%.
ideas.falsifier: Under 10% of presence calls fall below 30% of maximum (the film-relative bar already selects the strong regime); or accuracy differs by under 5 points between bins; or a word-overlap judge shows the same drop, so the bins differ in words, not meaning.
ideas.data: FineWeb sample (ODC-By): 10 million tokens for the bins, 100 million for the maxima of the tested units only. The study corpus of 3,700 Wikipedia plot sentences (CC BY-SA) and its 125 labelled units (study/results/labels.json, labels_wf.json). 500 word-matched and random active units as controls.
ideas.method: Maximum: largest value over general text and the study corpus; report its growth from 1 to 100 million tokens. Express each presence call as a fraction, flagging firings made by two negative parts multiplying. Blind judges match the label to a binned held-out sentence against a foil under 5% sharing as many of the label's words. Bootstrap over units.
ideas.rivals: Word-overlap judge per bin, embedding similarity of label to sentence, an LLM reading with no activations, random units through the same bins. Most dangerous: word overlap in the strong bin, because a name unit's strong firings are the name. Foils matched on word overlap are there to expose that.
ideas.premise: P1. If presence sits in the weak regime where labels fail, the study measured something its source essay does not vouch for, and the presence rule must change.
ideas.bio: Calling a gene expressed against its own baseline, not another tissue's
ideas.cost: S to M. One 10-million-token pass per model (about two hours), one 100-million-token pass tracking only the tested units (about a day unattended), about 4,000 judge calls.
ideas.payoff: A presence rule that does not depend on a reference set of films (a fixed fraction of the unit's own range), or evidence that the film-relative bar was adequate.
ideas.risk: Batman-specific units (names, places) may never meet their trigger in general text, so their range comes from the study corpus alone and the test says little about them.
ideas.review: Two repairs. Foils that merely contained the label's words made the weak bin harder by construction; foils are now matched on overlap. A 10-million-token maximum understates rare units, so maxima now use 100 million tokens plus the study corpus. Labels still come from Batman text.

ideas.title: One neuron, a few, a direction or a feature?
ideas.question: How many neurons does a story concept need, and does a random direction, a learned direction or a dictionary feature detect it better?
ideas.hypothesis: Averaged over 30 concepts, the best single neuron's held-out AUC (chance 0.5) on concept-without-its-words against words-without-the-concept is within 0.05 of the best 32-neuron set, and neurons beat random directions at equal count by at least 0.05.
ideas.falsifier: One neuron trails 32 by more than 0.10 on average (the unit is a set); or random directions match neurons at equal count; or a single dictionary feature beats the single neuron by 0.05 on average. Each unit type is scored after subtracting its own shuffled-label result.
ideas.data: The IN21 pairs and decoys. Llama Scope sparse autoencoders and transcoders (learned dictionaries of rarely active features; a transcoder imitates an MLP layer): 256 dictionaries on Llama-3.1-8B base, 32K and 128K features, Hugging Face, front card Apache-2.0. Gemma Scope transcoders for Gemma-2-2B, CC BY 4.0, as a small-model arm.
ideas.method: All unit types read at the same four depths of Llama-3.1-8B base at 8-bit, the model the dictionaries were trained on; the study's 4-bit instruct neurons are an extra arm. Rank units on development data and average the top k (1 to 128) without fitted weights. Add a difference-of-means residual direction. Held-out mixed-cell AUC against k, bootstrapped over concepts.
ideas.rivals: Logistic probe on a sentence embedding, TF-IDF classifier, zero-shot LLM reader, mean-pooled residual stream, all on the same mixed cells. Most dangerous: the difference-of-means direction, which beat dictionary features at detection in AxBench. If it wins, the meme unit should be a direction and neurons remain a cheap readout.
ideas.premise: P1. Decides whether 'a meme is one neuron' survives, becomes 'a small set', or gives way to directions or features; fixes the unit for later designs.
ideas.bio: Gene, operon or pathway: which level carries the trait
ideas.cost: M. Porting dictionary weights to MLX and checking reconstruction is the work; extraction takes minutes. About 1 to 2 weeks on the laptop.
ideas.payoff: An accuracy-against-size curve per unit type and a decision on which unit the rest of the registry should freeze.
ideas.risk: With about 100 development sentences per concept, larger sets are chosen noisily, which flatters single neurons. The dictionaries may reconstruct the 8-bit model poorly; report explained variance first.
ideas.review: Per-concept AUC on 20 against 20 items has an error near 0.08, so 'within 0.05' is now a pooled claim. Fitted probes on 100 sentences would overfit; replaced by unweighted top-k averages. Comparison moved to the base model the dictionaries were trained on. Depends on IN21.

ideas.title: Test-retest across independent retellings of one work
ideas.question: Is a unit's reading a stable property of a work, or of one summary of it?
ideas.hypothesis: For frozen concept units, the reading (the unit's score for a text) agrees between two independent summaries of the same story at a median intraclass correlation (0 none, 1 perfect) of at least 0.5, and at least 0.10 above word-matched control units.
ideas.falsifier: Median intraclass correlation under 0.3; or not above both word-matched units and the word-presence rival by 0.05; or no higher than for matched different-story pairs. Any of these means one summary cannot stand for a work.
ideas.data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 summaries of 29,505 stories from five Wikipedia language editions, with machine translations and name-anonymised versions; CC BY-SA 4.0. Sample 600 stories with an English and a translated summary of 20 or more sentences each, dropping pairs the dataset's similarity score marks as translations; plus 600 different-story pairs matched on genre, decade, length.
ideas.method: Units frozen beforehand: IN21's units, the study's labelled concept units, 2,000 random active and word-matched units. Readings on anonymised text, both summaries cut to equal sentence count. Per-unit intraclass correlation of the continuous reading (presence agreement is secondary, since presence is rare), same-story against different-story pairs, bootstrap over stories. 600 stories gives a standard error near 0.04.
ideas.rivals: Word-presence and TF-IDF agreement, story-embedding cosine (that model trained on this dataset, so use its test split), an LLM reader asked the label question on each summary, length alone. Most dangerous: the LLM reader. If it is more stable, neuron reliability still caps every validity figure we report.
ideas.premise: P1. Reliability bounds validity. Low agreement means the Batman grid measured Wikipedia summaries, not works; agreement above word-matched units supports a content reading.
ideas.bio: Technical replicates: sequencing the same sample twice
ideas.cost: S. 1,200 summaries per model, minutes of extraction; a day for sampling and the LLM-reader rival.
ideas.payoff: A reliability coefficient per unit class, and the correction needed to interpret every later correlation.
ideas.risk: The second summary is machine-translated, so register differs as well as content; and the dataset paper found 13 of 100 German-English pairs were direct translations, which the similarity filter only partly removes.
ideas.review: Dataset confirmed (download live, CC BY-SA 4.0). Its most common summary length is three sentences, so sampling now requires 20 or more. Added the dataset's own translation filter. Main statistic changed from rare binary presence to the continuous reading. Translation style stays mixed with retelling.

ideas.title: A multitrait-multimethod matrix with human raters
ideas.question: Do unit readings agree with human judgements of the same named trope more than with other tropes, and how close do they come to human-human agreement?
ideas.hypothesis: Against adjudicated human labels, frozen units reach AUC (chance 0.5) of 0.75 or more for the median trope; unit-human kappa (chance-corrected agreement), pooled over tropes, is within 0.15 of human-human kappa; and same-trope agreement exceeds different-trope entries in at least 90% of comparisons.
ideas.falsifier: Median AUC under 0.65; or same-trope unit-human agreement below different-trope same-method agreement; or units trail the TF-IDF classifier against the human labels.
ideas.data: TiMoS (Chang et al. 2021): TV Tropes labels for about 5,600 films, repository MIT; synopses from IMDb, licence unclear, so commit film names and labels only. Test: 300 name-masked synopses from held-out franchises, 15 tagged and 15 untagged per trope, 10 plot-event tropes including near neighbours (revenge rampage, disproportionate retribution, karmic death); two paid annotators and an adjudicator.
ideas.method: Tropes fixed by a written rule before any activations: events visible in a plot, not production trivia. Choose a unit and a 5-unit set per trope on development synopses in two stages; freeze. Fill a 10-trope by 6-method table (neurons in two models, keywords, embeddings, LLM reader, humans); apply Campbell and Fiske's four checks. Nulls: shuffled labels; popularity-matched films.
ideas.rivals: Keywords, TF-IDF logistic regression, a sentence-embedding probe and a trope-by-trope LLM reader are rows of the same table; length and popularity are covariates. Most dangerous: the LLM reader, though tropes proved hard for GPT-4. If it wins, the table still gives each method's validity against the human ceiling.
ideas.premise: P1. The first human evidence for or against the instrument. Losing to TF-IDF on human labels would leave P1 with inspectability only.
ideas.bio: Calibrating the 16S threshold against DNA-DNA hybridisation, the older standard
ideas.cost: L. About 40 annotator hours for whole synopses (roughly 800 US dollars), a day of compute, two weeks elapsed; needs a short ethics and consent note for paid raters.
ideas.payoff: Human-human agreement on trope presence, without which no model-human figure can be read, and a validity coefficient for every method.
ideas.risk: Humans reading synopses matched the TV Tropes labels at only F1 0.65 in the dataset's own paper, so human agreement may be too low to separate the methods; kappa errors per trope stay near 0.1.
ideas.review: Random passages would hold too few positives per trope, and labels are per film, so raters now read whole synopses, enriched by tag. Many TiMoS tropes are production trivia; a selection rule was added. Single neurons will probably fail; the human ceiling is the real payoff.

ideas.title: How much reading is length, position and wrapper?
ideas.question: What share of a unit's reading comes from the motif, and what share from text length, position, surrounding text and prompt wrapper?
ideas.hypothesis: For frozen units the motif accounts for at least 50% of reading variance, intraclass correlation (0 none, 1 perfect) across filler lengths is at least 0.75, and filler-only texts of 30 sentences fire at no more than 5% against a nominal 3%.
ideas.falsifier: Motif share under 30%; or false-fire rate on 30-sentence filler at or above 15%; or presence kappa (chance-corrected agreement) across wrappers under 0.6.
ideas.data: Scripted: for 10 IN21 concepts, 4 test concept sentences and their 4 matched controls, each set in 1, 5 or 30 filler sentences, early or late, under 4 wrappers: 1,920 texts plus 408 filler-only. Filler comes from 34 of the study's 69 ordinary film summaries (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA); the other 35 set the presence bar.
ideas.method: Units frozen from IN21, whether or not they passed. Wrappers: bare text, chat template, after an instruction, after unrelated text. Per unit, a variance-components model (how much each factor moves the score) with motif = own concept against matched control; report motif share, intraclass correlations and false-fire rates. Null: random and word-matched units through the same design.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and keywords (immune to position and wrapper by construction), whole-text and windowed sentence embeddings, an LLM reader, a length-only predictor. Most dangerous: TF-IDF, perfectly stable here. The test is whether neurons come close; if not, the study's whole-document, 40-sentence readings need redoing.
ideas.premise: P1. Shows whether presence reflects content or formatting; a fail would explain why sentence count alone scored 0.76 in the study's identity test (study/results/experiments.json).
ideas.bio: Batch effects: same sample, different lane or reagent lot
ideas.cost: S. Scripted assembly, about 2,300 short passes per model, one day.
ideas.payoff: A length-corrected reading rule and a list of formatting choices to fix in every later extraction.
ideas.risk: Filler from film summaries contains motifs of its own, inflating the false-fire rate; 34 independent filler films limit how precisely a 5% rate can be told from 3%.
ideas.review: The filler films also set the presence bar, which fixes the false-fire rate by construction; the films are now split. Matched controls added so 'motif share' is defined per unit. 50 sentences cut to 30, the most one film summary allows. Needs IN21 first.

ideas.title: Do units read known works differently from unseen ones?
ideas.question: Does a unit's reading of a plot change when the model already knows the work, compared with a work released after the model?
ideas.hypothesis: Agreement between a unit's reading of a Wikipedia plot and of its paraphrase, and of the plot with character names swapped for new ones, is the same for films the model recognises and films released after it: difference in kappa (chance-corrected agreement) under 0.05, with the 90% interval inside plus or minus 0.10.
ideas.falsifier: Kappa difference of 0.10 or more between recognised and unseen films on either alteration. A null result counts only if the positive control works: on 100 famous public-domain passages the model's token probability must be clearly higher for the verbatim text than for its paraphrase.
ideas.data: English Wikipedia plot sections (CC BY-SA 4.0): 300 films released after June 2025 (after Qwen3, April 2025, and Llama 3.1, 2024), original stories only, no sequels or adaptations; 300 films from 2005 to 2020 matched on genre and length. One paraphrase and one name-swapped version each; 60 checked by hand. 100 famous public-domain passages.
ideas.method: Units: frozen IN21 units, labelled concept units, 2,000 random active units; name detectors excluded. Split older films by whether the model names the film from its masked plot (the recognition check in preregistration/readers.py). Compare verbatim-paraphrase and verbatim-name-swap agreement across recognised, unrecognised and post-release films (difference in differences), bootstrap over films.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and word presence (cannot recall anything; they show the loss from paraphrase alone), sentence embeddings, an LLM reader that may recognise the film. Most dangerous: paraphrase damage, equal in all groups by design. If no effect appears, the Batman readings stand as content readings on this point.
ideas.premise: P1. A recognition effect would mean readings on famous works are partly recall, weakening every Wikipedia-based result; no effect removes a standing objection.
ideas.bio: Reference bias: reads matching the reference genome map better
ideas.cost: S to M. 1,800 texts per model, minutes of extraction, 1,200 rewriting calls and a recognition pass; 3 days.
ideas.payoff: Whether future tests must use works released after the models, or Wikipedia text is safe.
ideas.risk: Recent films differ from older ones in summary style and length, which matching cannot fully remove; the number of eligible post-release original films was not confirmed.
ideas.review: Release date is a weak stand-in for memorisation: an 8B model has not memorised most older plots. Added a per-film recognition split, a name-swap arm (recall keyed by names is the real Batman threat), a positive control and an equivalence margin. Sequels and adaptations are now excluded.

ideas.title: Same neurons at 4-bit, 8-bit and full precision?
ideas.question: Do the same unit indices give the same readings and presence calls when the model is not quantised to 4 bits?
ideas.hypothesis: Between the 4-bit and full-precision builds, the median per-unit correlation of sentence readings is at least 0.95, presence kappa (chance-corrected agreement) is at least 0.9, and at least 70% of a unit's 20 strongest sentences are shared.
ideas.falsifier: Median correlation under 0.9, presence kappa under 0.73 (the study's cross-model kappa, study/results/robustness/nulls.json), or top-20 overlap under 50%. Any of these makes 4-bit quantisation a first-order confound and blocks borrowing published labels or dictionaries made at full precision.
ideas.data: The study corpus (3,700 Wikipedia plot sentences, CC BY-SA) and 1 million tokens of FineWeb (ODC-By). MLX builds of Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 4-bit, 8-bit and bf16 (16-bit floats), all on Hugging Face under the Apache-2.0 and Llama 3.1 licences.
ideas.method: Units: the study's 125 labelled units, IN21's frozen units and 5,000 random active units, by layer third. Same text through each build; per-unit Pearson correlation of sentence readings, kappa of presence under the frozen rule, overlap of the 20 strongest sentences. Null: a different unit in the same layer, which gives the chance level. 5,000 units make every interval narrow.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF, embeddings and an LLM reader do not depend on these weights, so they are perfectly stable here and cannot lose. The bar is therefore the study's cross-model agreement and the chance level from mismatched units. Most dangerous outcome: weak-regime readings shift while strong ones hold, which IN23 would then explain.
ideas.premise: P1. A pass lets the study's 4-bit units inherit evidence gathered at full precision (public neuron descriptions, Llama Scope dictionaries, the source essay). A fail means every reading so far is specific to one quantised file.
ideas.bio: Checking a low-coverage sequencing run against a deep one
ideas.cost: S. Six extraction passes of under an hour each. The bf16 builds are about 16 GB and may not fit beside their activations on a 24 GB laptop; if so, 8-bit is the reference. One day.
ideas.payoff: A stated precision limit for the instrument, and permission (or not) to reuse public neuron labels and dictionaries.
ideas.risk: Likely an uneventful pass: Singh and Sajjad found no drastic neuron-level change from 4-bit quantisation in other models, though they did not track individual units' strongest examples.
ideas.review: Promoted from a seed: it is cheap, and IN24 and any reuse of full-precision labels depend on it. All six builds confirmed on Hugging Face. Weakness: covers MLX quantisation only, and prior work points to a pass, so it is informative mainly if it fails.

ideas.title: Do units add anything to the cheap readers?
ideas.question: On natural synopses with human-named tropes, do frozen unit readings improve held-out trope detection once word, embedding, LLM-reader and length scores are already in the model?
ideas.hypothesis: Adding 16 frozen units per trope to a combined model of the cheap readers raises median held-out AUC (chance 0.5) across about 30 plot-event tropes by at least 0.02, with the interval excluding zero, in both 8B models, and by more than 16 random active units do.
ideas.falsifier: Gain under 0.01, or no larger than the gain from random or word-matched units, while the cheap readers add 0.05 or more to the units alone. Then units carry nothing about tropes that cheap readers lack.
ideas.data: TiMoS (Chang et al. 2021): TV Tropes labels for about 5,600 films in training, validation and test files (4,059, 715 and 825); the median trope is tagged on about 375 films. Repository MIT; synopses from IMDb, licence unclear, so commit film names and labels only. Names masked by script; films re-split by franchise.
ideas.method: Per trope, pick units on the training split in two stages; freeze. On the validation split fit two logistic models: cheap readers only (TF-IDF classifier score, embedding probe score, LLM reader's yes-probability, length, number of tropes tagged as a popularity proxy) and the same plus units. Compare held-out AUC, bootstrap over films; and in reverse. Null: shuffled trope labels.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF logistic regression, a sentence-embedding probe, a zero-shot LLM reader, synopsis length, popularity, the mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: the embedding probe, trained on thousands of films. If units add nothing, P1 keeps inspectability and cost only, which is worth knowing before any lineage work.
ideas.premise: P1. The discriminant rung on natural text at scale. An increment in both models would be the first evidence that neurons carry narrative content cheap readers miss; none would repeat the Batman result on 5,600 films.
ideas.bio: Does a new biomarker add to the standard panel?
ideas.cost: M. About two hours of extraction per model; the LLM reader on validation and test films for 30 tropes is the heavy part, about a day; one week in all.
ideas.payoff: A number for what neurons add beyond cheap readers on human-named memes, per trope, with the reverse comparison.
ideas.risk: Crowd labels are noisy and a missing tag is not absence, which shrinks every method's score and may hide a small increment.
ideas.review: Added: the area had no stand-alone discriminant test on natural text. Label files checked: 5,599 films, trope prevalence 4 to 33%. Weakness: TV Tropes tags track popularity and miss true cases, and Kantamneni et al. suggest no increment is the likely result.

ideas.title: Natural 2x2 on expert motif annotations
ideas.question: On sentences experts marked for a motif, does a unit separate the motif without its index words from the words without the motif?
ideas.note: Alyami and Finlayson 2026: 2,670 motif expressions, 200 motifs, 58,450 sentence-motif pairs from the Arabian Nights. Blocked for now: annotated on a modern translation still in copyright, and the data is promised only on acceptance. Rivals: BM25, embeddings, and their fine-tuned Llama 3 at F1 0.85. GOLEM covers motif mentions in news, not tales.

ideas.title: Concept-cell invariance for name units
ideas.question: Does a character unit fire on aliases and name-free descriptions, and stay silent on the same token in another sense?
ideas.note: About 24 name units; hand-written aliases, descriptions and homonyms (robin the bird, joker the card). Rival: a token-match dictionary. The Lucius Fox unit firing on Zorro's 'Fox' suggests a fail.

ideas.title: Can frozen units register an invented trope?
ideas.question: Does any unit or small set separate stories carrying a trope invented after training from matched controls?
ideas.note: 20 invented tropes by 10 stories. Rivals: a sentence-embedding centroid from three examples and an LLM given three examples. A fail limits neuron memetics to memes the model already knows.

ideas.title: Dose-response on assembled long texts
ideas.question: Does a unit's reading rise with the number of planted instances of its motif, independent of text length?
ideas.note: Doses 0, 1, 2, 5 built from IN21 items. Rivals: TF-IDF counts, length alone, an LLM reader with recursive summaries. Fails if rank correlation with dose is under 0.5 or length does as well.

ideas.title: Whole pipeline on a model that learned nothing
ideas.question: Do discovery, labelling, canon and tree steps yield 'memes' from a weight-shuffled model or from the token-embedding layer alone?
ideas.note: Uses the study corpus unchanged. If the controls match the real model's label-test or canon figures, those figures reflect the texts, not learned units. IN22 already runs the shuffled model through its coherence test.

ideas.title: Same threshold, other language and era
ideas.question: Given the same human label, does a unit fire at the same rate in translated and period-styled text?
ideas.note: Logistic regression of firing on label, group and interaction; pass if group odds ratios stay within 0.67 to 1.5 for three quarters of units. Rival: a multilingual sentence encoder. Protocols exist in preregistration/, deferred.

ideas.title: Do Batman-corpus labels survive general text?
ideas.question: Does a unit relabelled from its top examples on general text, and from Transluce's public Llama descriptions, keep the label it got from 3,700 Batman-heavy sentences?
ideas.note: Bolukbasi's corpus-shift check. Rival: the unit's best single word. More than a third of labels changing would mean in-corpus labelling is unsafe. Transluce described the full-precision model, so run IN29 first.

ideas.title: Do two labellers give a unit the same label?
ideas.question: Do independent labellers, each shown a different half of a unit's strongest examples, give labels that a blind judge calls the same?
ideas.note: Added by review. A second AI reading renamed 5 of 26 units (study/results/labels.json against labels_wf.json). Use two model families and one human on the 125 labelled units. Rival: the unit's best single word as its label. Agreement under 60% means labels are not a property of the unit.

ideas.title: Held-out twin census with word-matched nulls
ideas.question: What share of Qwen3-8B units have a Llama-3.1-8B twin on unseen text once words, sentence length and position in the plot are accounted for?
ideas.hypothesis: At least 2% of sampled Qwen units have a twin (the best-correlated Llama unit, chosen on other films) whose held-out correlation beats a rotation baseline by 0.5. At least half of those keep a partial correlation of 0.3 after the word, length and position predictors are removed, mostly at 40 to 60% depth.
ideas.falsifier: Fewer than 0.5% of units pass, or fewer than one passer in ten keeps partial correlation 0.3, on original and name-masked text alike. Either refutes neuron-level P2 beyond shared vocabulary. Between 0.5% and 2% is inconclusive. A layer-stratified sample of 20,000 units gives a standard error near 0.1 percentage points.
ideas.data: The 1,000 random film plots already committed (`preregistration/sources/t3_random_films.jsonl.gz`; 22,225 sentences after the 40-sentence cap; Wikipedia text, CC BY-SA 4.0). A name-masked copy is not committed: make it with an open entity tagger and hand-check 200 sentences for leaks. Split by film: 500 to choose twins, 500 to score. No Batman text.
ideas.method: Unit: each sign of each MLP channel (a hidden neuron), strongest value per sentence. For each sampled Qwen unit, pick the best-correlated Llama unit on one half, keeping mutual picks; score on the other half. Statistics: correlation above a random rotation of Llama's layer (Gurnee's baseline); partial correlation given word, length and position predictors. Null: sentences misaligned between models.
ideas.rivals: Each Qwen unit is also predicted from its best single word, a 10-word lasso (a regression that keeps few words), a ridge fit on all words and word pairs, a sentence-embedding ridge, sentence length and position, and Llama's mean-pooled residual stream; an LLM reader only for labelled units. The all-word ridge is most dangerous: if it wins, twins are vocabulary.
ideas.premise: P2. A pass gives a counted core of shared units to seed a common catalogue. A fail means 'the same neurons' gives way to 'the same directions', and twin strength stops being a mark of a real meme, because it selects word detectors.
ideas.bio: Orthologue census by reciprocal best hits.
ideas.cost: S. Four extraction passes of under ten minutes each (two models, two text versions), a few hours of correlation on the laptop, no API spend. Stored whole, the activations take about 80 GB, so process them layer by layer.
ideas.payoff: The first cross-family neuron census on 8B models, with held-out numbers to replace the in-sample 0.82 and 0.40 (`nulls.json`, `phylo.json.gz`), and a list of beyond-word shared units that every later cross-model design reuses. The study's 125 labelled units and 27 concept units are scored as fixed subgroups.
ideas.risk: The pass share moves with the 0.5 threshold, which Gurnee et al. say has no principled value, so the whole curve is reported. A word control fitted on 11,000 sentences can miss rare synonyms and inflate the beyond-word share; known single-word detectors (best-word correlation 0.9 or more) should fail the test, and their pass rate measures that leak.
ideas.review: Added sentence length and plot position to the controls (shared position detectors would otherwise pass as beyond-word twins), an all-word control, and a leak check on known word detectors. The name-masked copy does not exist yet. Remaining weakness: rare synonyms can slip past any word control.

ideas.title: Same story, another language, another model
ideas.question: When a story is retold in another language and no words are shared, do unit readings still match, within one model and between Qwen and Llama?
ideas.hypothesis: On name-replaced summaries, units find the same story across languages (German original against an English summary) at half or more of the rate they reach when both are read in English; the measure is top-1, the right story ranked first among all test stories. Qwen reading German against Llama reading English keeps half or more of the within-model rate.
ideas.falsifier: The cross-language rate is under a quarter of the same-language rate, or no better than random units matched on firing rate, or the cross-model rate is under a quarter of the within-model rate. At least 1,000 qualifying test stories (count them before registering) make a 5-point paired gap about 3 standard errors.
ideas.data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 Wikipedia plot summaries of 29,505 stories in English, German, French, Italian and Spanish, with supplied machine translations into English, name-replaced versions and an 80/10/10 split (test: 2,951 stories). A 1.7 GB download; text CC BY-SA 4.0, code MIT. Summaries under 8 sentences and pairs flagged as direct translations are dropped.
ideas.method: Three contrasts per story: German original against its supplied English translation (language only); English summary against the translated German summary (retelling only); English against German original (both). Units: those stable across language on the development split. Cross-model link: a ridge map (a regularised linear fit) from development stories; UN21 twins second. A hard gallery uses same-genre, same-decade stories.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF on the supplied English translations (machine translation makes words a rival again), multilingual sentence embeddings, an LLM asked whether two summaries tell one story (500 pairs), length difference, random units, and each model's mean-pooled residual stream. Multilingual embeddings will probably win. The result still shows whether unit agreement exists once shared vocabulary is gone.
ideas.premise: Both. Agreement that survives translation would be the first cross-model evidence that is not names and words. A collapse means the study's agreement was lexical, and translation-proof memes need directions or embeddings. Replaces the deferred Chinese protocol with human-written text in languages Llama 3.1 lists as supported.
ideas.bio: Synonymous codons: different sequence, same protein.
ideas.cost: M. About a week: a data loader, name replacement for the non-English originals, five to ten hours of extraction for two models, no paid API because translations are supplied.
ideas.payoff: An answer to Mike's fuzziness question at story scale: retelling, translation and name removal are separated in one natural corpus of thousands of stories instead of 32 works. French, Italian and Spanish repeat the German result.
ideas.risk: Both models have read these pages in every language and may simply recognise the film, so stories neither model can name are scored separately. Language editions tell different parts of a story. Leftover names, numbers and cognates (words with a shared root) can leak, and translation errors can hide signal.
ideas.review: Defined the unit choice, replaced the dependence on UN21 twins with a fitted map, fixed an impossible gallery and added a recognition check. Dataset confirmed. Remaining: the supplied name-replaced texts are probably English only, and language-general middle layers within one model are already reported (Anthropic 2025).
sources: Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again, LREC-COLING)
Anthropic 2025 (On the Biology of a Large Language Model)

ideas.title: Carrying a reading from Qwen into Llama's catalogue
ideas.question: Can a tale read by Qwen be matched against a library of tales read by Llama, using a map fitted only on unrelated film text?
ideas.hypothesis: Carried by a ridge map (a regularised linear fit) fitted on film sentences, Qwen's readings of name-masked tales find same-type tales in Llama's library with 80% or more of the above-chance precision Llama reaches when it reads the queries itself. Single twins keep under 50%.
ideas.falsifier: The ridge-carried reading keeps under 50% of Llama's own above-chance precision, or does no better than a map fitted on misaligned sentences (sign-flip test across 81 tale types; about 80% power for a 0.03 gap if type differences vary by 0.1). Then a catalogue cannot be shared by mapping.
ideas.data: Annotated Folktales in the `trilogy` repository (Hagedorn and Darányi, Zenodo 6575263; the repository states CC BY-SA 4.0): 1,518 English tales, each given one of 182 Aarne-Thompson-Uther tale types by the folklorist D. L. Ashliman. Without 20 tales marked non-commercial, 81 types have 8 or more tellings (1,066 tales): the test set. Types with 4 to 7 tellings are for development.
ideas.method: Each name-masked tale is read as in the study (top sentences per unit) and as a mid-depth residual-stream vector (the state passed between layers). Qwen's reading is carried into Llama's coordinates by single twins, a 10-unit lasso, full-layer ridge, a rotation, or anchor similarities with no fitting. Statistic: average precision of same-type retrieval. Null: maps fitted on misaligned sentences.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF similarity (needs no map), a sentence-embedding model, an LLM asked whether two tales share a type (subsample), tale length, random units carried the same way, and Llama's pooled residual stream reading the queries itself. TF-IDF is most dangerous; if it wins on precision, retention still settles whether maps work. Same-type pairs with low word overlap are scored separately.
ideas.premise: P2. Retention by ridge but not by twins supports P2 restated as shared directions and makes one catalogue practical. Low retention by every map means one catalogue per model, which is Mike's fallback of a single reference model.
ideas.bio: Lifting gene annotations from one genome to another.
ideas.cost: S. Under an hour of extraction for both models (tales capped at 40 sentences); maps and retrieval in a day or two on the laptop; LLM reading on a subsample.
ideas.payoff: How much of a reading survives a change of model, for each kind of map, and whether a meme travels as one neuron, a few neurons or a direction. Readings of texts that cannot be redistributed could then be shared and used with another model.
ideas.risk: Tale types share key nouns (hare, slipper), so TF-IDF may sit near the ceiling and leave the maps little room to differ. A film-fitted map may fail on nineteenth-century folktale prose because the text differs, not the models; a map fitted on development tales measures that. Both models have probably read these tales.
ideas.review: Rebuilt as retrieval. Picking a detector from 900,000 units on four tellings would overfit, as the study's Qwen revenge unit did; now no unit is chosen on tale labels. Counts confirmed from the file. Remaining: labels come from one folklorist, and tale types may be too lexical.

ideas.title: Precision and size ladder within Qwen3
ideas.question: How much does a unit's reading change with weight precision and model size, compared with the change between model families?
ideas.hypothesis: Between 4-bit and 8-bit Qwen3-8B, the same unit's sentence responses correlate at a median of 0.95 or more, and work-level presence agrees at kappa 0.9 or more (agreement corrected for chance). Secondary: the share of units with beyond-word Llama twins (UN21) rises with size from Qwen3-0.6B to 14B, rank correlation 0.9 or more.
ideas.falsifier: Presence kappa between 4-bit and 8-bit is under 0.8 for meme units, close to the 0.73 found between Qwen and Llama for the 31 named memes (`nulls.json`). Secondary: the rank correlation of twin share with size is under 0.9 (five sizes reach 0.9 by chance about 1 time in 24). Sample: 25,925 sentences in 1,114 works.
ideas.data: The committed study corpus (114 works, 3,700 sentences, original and name-free) and the 1,000 committed random film plots (22,225 sentences); Wikipedia text, CC BY-SA. Models: open Qwen3 weights at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B (Apache 2.0, confirmed on Hugging Face), at 4-bit, 8-bit and 16-bit precision wherever they fit in 24 GB.
ideas.method: Precision arm: one unit index read at two precisions on the same text, so wording cannot differ; sentence correlation, presence kappa, whether the 56 core and 31 named memes are selected again, and the same for the 8-bit storage of activations. Size arm: UN21's held-out census between each Qwen3 size and Llama. Nulls: rate-matched unit pairs; misaligned sentences.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and text length do not change with precision (kappa 1), so they set the ceiling. The mean-pooled residual stream goes through the same comparison and is most dangerous: if it is stable where single units are not, the unit basis is the fragile part. Random non-meme units show whether meme units are more or less stable than average.
ideas.premise: Both. Stable readings mean the 4-bit study stands as measured; unstable ones mean every published unit number carries unmeasured noise, and no cross-model agreement can exceed that ceiling. A twin share that grows with size supports convergence with scale; a flat one sides with Koepke et al. against it.
ideas.bio: Technical replicates before comparing species.
ideas.cost: S. An hour or two of extraction per model and precision. The 14B model at 4 bits is the largest that fits beside its activations; the 8B model at 16 bits (about 16 GB) may not fit, but 1.7B and 4B at 16 bits do.
ideas.payoff: A reliability figure for the instrument itself, which the study never measured, and a ceiling against which every cross-model agreement number can be read.
ideas.risk: The likely result is dull: readings are stable, which is still worth knowing. Unit indices line up across precisions but not across sizes, so the size arm inherits every weakness of twin matching, has one model per size, and Llama's fixed 8B size may favour the 8B Qwen whatever the trend.
ideas.review: Made precision the primary arm and size a stated secondary with its own small-sample test; dropped the claim that this tests whether neurons are clean. All checkpoints confirmed. Remaining: five sizes with one model each cannot separate scale from similarity to Llama's own size.

ideas.title: Shared units against human judgements of similarity
ideas.question: Do the units two models share predict which texts people judge alike better than the units only one model has?
ideas.hypothesis: Across sentence pairs rated by people, distance over shared units tracks the human score better than distance over model-specific units, by 0.05 or more in rank correlation after word overlap and length are removed. On story triples, shared units pick the story the annotators chose more often.
ideas.falsifier: The gap in partial rank correlation is under 0.02, or the shared-unit term adds nothing once word overlap is in the regression (p above 0.05). 8,628 pairs give a standard error near 0.01. The 1,039 story triples can only detect a gap of 5 to 6 points, so they cannot refute alone.
ideas.data: STS Benchmark (Cer et al. 2017): 8,628 English sentence pairs with human similarity scores; no licence is stated on its dataset card, so confirm it and commit ids only. SemEval-2026 Task 4 (Hatzel et al. 2026): 1,039 story-summary triples with human choices (200 development, 800 test); confirm the licence on the task site before registering.
ideas.method: Qwen and Llama read each text. Shared units pass UN21's held-out, beyond-word twin test. Model-specific units have no twin and are matched on layer, firing rate, word-predictability and stability across precision (UN24). Statistics: partial rank correlation of unit distance with the human score; triple accuracy; both repeated where word overlap and the human score disagree. Null: random unit sets.
ideas.rivals: Word overlap and TF-IDF, a general sentence embedding (trained on such data, it will win outright), an LLM asked directly (subsample), length difference, random units, and each model's pooled residual stream, the dangerous one for units. The design still shows whether cross-model agreement marks the part of a reading people share.
ideas.premise: P2, and the bridge to readers. A pass supports the convergence argument: what models agree on is what people see, so twin strength could filter for real memes. A fail means cross-model agreement and human relevance are separate properties, so universality cannot stand in for human validation.
ideas.bio: Sequence conserved across species as a sign of function.
ideas.cost: S. Short texts, two extraction passes, archived human labels, no new raters. Needs the unit lists from UN21 and UN24 first.
ideas.payoff: The first check of any unit reading in this project against human judgement, at no rater cost, and a test of whether twin strength is a useful filter for memes people would recognise.
ideas.risk: Sentence pairs from captions and headlines are far from story memes. The story triples are few, were kept only where two LLMs disagreed, and annotators agreed weakly (alpha 0.33). Units without twins may simply be noisier, which matching can only partly remove.
ideas.review: The story triples alone were fatal: 1,039 in all, kept only where LLMs disagree, annotator agreement 0.33, best system 78%. Added 8,628 rated sentence pairs for power and a stability-matched control. Remaining: depends on UN21 and UN24, and sentence similarity is not story similarity.

ideas.title: Text-chosen units read from pixels in one model
ideas.question: Does a unit that responds to a scene described in words respond to the same scene shown as an image with no lettering?
ideas.hypothesis: In Qwen3-VL-8B, 30% or more of units that agree across two people's captions of an image (correlation 0.5 or more) also agree between caption and pixels at 0.3 or more on unseen images, against under 5% for mismatched unit pairs.
ideas.falsifier: Under 10% of caption-reliable units transfer to pixels, or no more than mismatched unit pairs matched on firing rate, or transfer vanishes on images with no detected lettering. Then unit readings are bound to text. 1,800 held-out images give a per-unit correlation standard error near 0.024.
ideas.data: Crossmodal-3600 (Thapliyal et al. 2022): 3,600 photographs from around the world with human captions in 36 languages, written independently and not translated; captions CC BY 4.0 (17 MB), images 302 MB with an attribution file. Half the images to choose units, half to score. Typographic decoys (a caption rendered as an image) are generated.
ideas.method: Model: Qwen3-VL-8B at 4 bits, whose language layers have the same shape as the study's Qwen3-8B; first measure whether a unit index gives the same reading of text in both. Read every unit on caption tokens with no image, and on image tokens with a neutral prompt. Per unit: caption-to-caption, caption-to-pixel and caption-to-decoy correlation. Nulls: mismatched unit pairs; shuffled images.
ideas.rivals: In one task, finding an image's own caption among 1,800: text-chosen units reading pixels against a contrastive image-text model (CLIP or SigLIP), the model's own written caption matched by TF-IDF, its pooled residual stream, and image brightness and size as the analogue of length. CLIP will win retrieval; the transfer share still says whether a text catalogue reads images.
ideas.premise: P1 mainly, P2 across media. Transfer means units pass the concept-cell test of invariance (one response to a word and a picture), which name detectors fail. No transfer means one catalogue per medium, and the poster experiment cannot be joined to the text study.
ideas.bio: Concept cells that fire to a face and its written name.
ideas.cost: M. New extraction code for a vision-language model, then a few hours of compute for 3,600 images and their captions.
ideas.payoff: Whether one catalogue can read both text and images, whether the study's own Qwen3-8B units carry over to pictures, and a controlled replacement for the poster experiment, which had no cheap rival and no lettering control.
ideas.risk: Captions describe concrete scenes, so a pass shows invariance for objects and places, the easy case, and says little about story memes such as revenge or a secret identity. A model trained to caption images may fire word units on pixels simply because it is about to write the word.
ideas.review: Switched to Qwen3-VL-8B (checkpoint confirmed; same layer count and widths as Qwen3-8B) so the study's own units can be tested, and put the rivals into one retrieval task. Remaining: units shared between text and image are already reported for such models, and photographs are far from story memes.

ideas.title: Steered in Qwen, read in Llama
ideas.question: When Qwen is steered to write a meme with its usual words blocked, does the matching Llama unit detect it in the text?
ideas.hypothesis: For 100 Qwen units with beyond-word twins, passages written under steering (the unit's activation raised during writing) are traced to the right unit by Llama's twin readings at 20% top-1 or better (chance 1%), and at half or more of that rate when each unit's ten best words are banned from the output.
ideas.falsifier: Top-1 is under 5% with words banned, or no better than for matched Qwen units that lack a beyond-word twin, steered the same way. Then twin agreement does not survive when the meme is set by intervention. 100 units by 20 passages give 2,000 trials and a standard error under 1 point.
ideas.data: Generated by the experiment, no outside data: for each of 100 Qwen3-8B units (from UN21's list and the study's labelled concept units), 20 short story continuations from neutral prompts with the unit raised, the same for 100 matched comparison units, and unsteered controls. About 6,000 passages of 60 words, released under CC BY 4.0.
ideas.method: Ground truth: which unit was raised. Qwen writes; Llama only reads. Each passage is assigned to the unit whose Llama twin responds most, scaled by the unsteered controls. Word ban: the unit's ten best words (UN21's lasso) cannot be output. Steering strength is set on separate development units, and a blind LLM check confirms the text stays fluent.
ideas.rivals: Given half the passages for training: a TF-IDF classifier, a sentence-embedding classifier, and an LLM reader shown the unit labels. Also word overlap with each unit's top sentences, passage length, and Llama's pooled residual stream. TF-IDF is most dangerous without the ban, the embedding classifier with it. Twins get no training passages, so a tie favours twins.
ideas.premise: Both. The only test in this area where the meme in a text is known by construction. A pass shows a unit means the same thing when written by one model and read by another. A fail alongside a pass in UN21 means twins share inputs, not meaning.
ideas.bio: A gene moved into another species and still expressed there.
ideas.cost: S to M. A steering hook is a few lines in the existing recorder (`study/extract.py`); about five hours of generation on the laptop, minutes of reading, and a small LLM check.
ideas.payoff: Causal evidence for or against P2 at unit level, and the first steering result of any kind in this project. Cammarata's essay uses steering as the direct test of a unit's label, and the study never ran it.
ideas.risk: Units that read a concept often do not write it, and raising a single unit in a 4-bit 8B model may produce nothing or nonsense; the share of steerable units is itself a result. With words banned, steering may fail outright, leaving nothing for Llama to read.
ideas.review: Added: no design in the area had a causal check, and this seed was the only one with ground truth set by intervention. Remaining weakness: single-unit steering may fail on most units, and steering transfer between models by learned maps is already reported (Agarwal 2026), though not this reading test.

ideas.title: Crosscoder latents against neurons on heredity
ideas.question: Do the shared latents of a joint Qwen-Llama dictionary recover documented sources on name-free text beyond words, where Qwen's neurons failed?
ideas.note: A crosscoder is one sparse dictionary that reads both models. Jiralerspong and Bricken 2026 trained one on this exact pair and say the training code is public; released weights were not confirmed, so budget 2 to 5 GPU days.
