Rivals: TF-IDF, word presence and sentence embeddings in the same residual test. Standard crosscoders lean towards calling features shared (Minder et al. 2025).

ideas.title: Mapped revenge direction
ideas.question: If Llama's revenge direction is carried into Qwen by a paired linear map, does Qwen detect revenge without the word, where its own unit scored 4 of 12?
ideas.note: Uses the 12 committed minimal pairs (`study/results/wording.json`) plus about 200 new ones checked by hand. Rivals: a sentence-embedding prototype and an LLM yes/no. One day on the laptop.

ideas.title: Trilingual brain check
ideas.question: Do units shared across models explain brain responses to one story heard in English, Chinese and French beyond word rate, position and static word embeddings?
ideas.note: Le Petit Prince fMRI corpus (Li et al. 2022, Scientific Data 9:530, public). Use contiguous train-test splits, as Feghhi et al. and Hadidi et al. require. Guo et al. 2026 already report sparse-autoencoder features of Llama-3.1-8B against brain data in these three languages, so the new part is cross-model units and the word-level controls. Expect a null; needs someone who knows fMRI encoding models. Cost M to L.

ideas.title: Does universality select for words?
ideas.question: How much of the variation in twin strength is explained by how word-like a unit is?
ideas.note: Hours, no model runs: per-unit fields are committed for 71 memes, not 200 (`study/results/robustness/nulls.json`, `f2_agreement/per_meme`); the rest need exporting. Rival predictor: best-word correlation alone. If it explains most of twin strength, twin strength is a poor filter for real memes.

ideas.title: Third family and second checkpoint
ideas.question: Is Qwen-Llama agreement typical of any two models, or does it change with a third family or a second checkpoint of one family?
ideas.note: Separates shared training text from convergence. The study found Qwen3-1.7B agreed with Qwen3-8B no better than Llama did (median 0.40 in both, `study/results/phylo.json.gz`). Gemma or Mistral at 4 bits fit the laptop. Same held-out and word-matched nulls as UN21.

ideas.title: Where the two models disagree
ideas.question: Are the units with no twin in the other model concentrated in culturally or politically loaded content?
ideas.note: Jiralerspong and Bricken 2026 report Chinese-state-aligned features exclusive to Qwen3-8B and American-exceptionalism features exclusive to Llama. Compare twinless units on neutral plots against history or news text. Rival: topic words. Tells users when the choice of reference model matters.

ideas.title: Story memes in generated scenes
ideas.question: Does one unit fire for a story meme stated in text and shown in a generated image with decoys and masked lettering?
ideas.note: Follow-up to UN26 for narrative memes such as a secret identity. Ground truth by construction, with a human check of a sample. Rivals: CLIP zero-shot, a captioner plus TF-IDF, the model asked directly.

ideas.title: Two languages, one photograph, no translator
ideas.question: Do units agree between English and German captions that two people wrote separately for the same photograph?
ideas.note: Crossmodal-3600 has captions written independently in 36 languages for 3,600 images (CC BY 4.0). A check on UN22 that is free of machine-translation artefacts, with Qwen reading German against Llama reading English as the cross-model step. Rivals: multilingual sentence embeddings, TF-IDF after translation, caption length. Concrete scenes only. Hours.

ideas.title: Scrambled sentences
ideas.question: How much twin agreement survives when the words of each sentence are shuffled, so that only the bag of words is left?
ideas.note: Reread UN21's film sentences with word order shuffled inside each sentence. Agreement that survives is carried by vocabulary alone; the drop is the share that needs word order. A check on UN21's word control that fits no model. Rival: TF-IDF, which shuffling leaves unchanged. Under a day.

ideas.title: Scientific memes along citations, with shared words controlled
ideas.question: Does a paper carry the neuron units of a paper it cites more than those of an uncited paper whose wording is just as close?
ideas.hypothesis: On held-out pairs where an uncited same-year decoy is matched to the cited paper on TF-IDF similarity (word overlap weighted by rarity; within 0.02), units pick the cited paper at least 60% of the time (chance 50%), and at least 2 points more often than random units with the same firing rate.
ideas.falsifier: Unit accuracy under 55%, or within 1 point of random units, on 20,000 held-out pairs from at least 4,000 citing papers (standard error roughly 0.5 points when resampled by citing paper). A second failure after Batman would settle that neurons add nothing to words for descent.
ideas.data: SNAP cit-HepTh: 27,770 physics papers with abstracts and all 352,807 citation links among them, 1993 to 2003 (checked 2026-11-08; no licence stated, so commit only IDs). Second field: about 30,000 biomedical abstracts with links from OpenAlex (CC0 per its documentation; needs a free key, anonymous access was refused on 2026-11-08).
ideas.method: Unit: a feed-forward neuron (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B), present when it fires strongly. Re-derive Kuhn's propagation score for units and n-grams. Pick the 2,000 best-propagating units on early links. On later links between papers unseen in tuning, sharing no author, count units shared with the cited paper and with the decoy. Repeat without word-detector units. Null: time-preserving link shuffle.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and BM25 (near 50% by design), Kuhn's n-gram score, a general sentence embedding, a citation-trained embedding (SPECTER2) as ceiling, an LLM reading 2,000 pairs, length, random units, the model's averaged internal state, open sparse-autoencoder features if available. The general embedding is most dangerous: popular ones were trained on citation pairs. If it wins, heredity past words stands, without units.
ideas.premise: P1. A pass is the first evidence on natural text at scale that units follow inherited ideas past the wording. A fail, added to Batman, leaves P1 without practical content for descent. Agreement between the two models bears weakly on P2.
ideas.bio: Parent-offspring resemblance against relatedness-matched controls
ideas.cost: M. About 400,000 sentences, a few hours per model on a laptop; most of the two weeks goes on assembling links and matching decoys.
ideas.payoff: Whether Kuhn's finding survives word matching when it is measured in units, and a reusable heredity benchmark with tens of thousands of documented links, the scale Batman lacked.
ideas.risk: A citation is weak evidence that an idea was inherited; most references are background. Matching on TF-IDF leaves shared subtopic; a second decoy set, co-cited with the source by a third paper, tests that. Close decoys exist mainly for loosely related citations, so the test pairs may not be typical.
ideas.review: Added a closed, key-free corpus (cit-HepTh) so Kuhn's score can be re-derived; split by paper, dropped shared-author pairs, added random-unit and co-cited-decoy checks. Remaining: a citation is weak evidence of inheritance, and embeddings trained on citation pairs will probably beat units.
sources: Edmonds 2002, Three challenges for the survival of memetics

ideas.title: Sperber's test: are retold ideas copied or rebuilt
ideas.question: When a story is retold down a chain, is its new content a copying error passed on to later retellings, or something each chain adds independently because every teller rebuilds the story the same way?
ideas.hypothesis: The memetic prediction: of the units a story gains by step 8, those inherited from the chain's own step 4 and absent from sibling chains outnumber those that also arose in sibling chains by at least 2 to 1. A step-8 retelling is matched to its own step-4 ancestor among six siblings at least 50% of the time (chance 17%).
ideas.falsifier: A copied-to-rebuilt ratio of 1 or less, with a bootstrap interval lying below 2, in both reader models, over 360 test chains from 60 stories (resampled by story; E3 had 15 works) and at least 2,000 gains; or matching under 30%. That is Sperber's outcome: new content is convergent, so shared units cannot be read as descent.
ideas.data: Built for the test and released with its lineage. 80 new 300-word stories without proper names, written from randomly drawn plot elements (20 for tuning, 60 for scoring). Each starts 6 chains that share only the seed. A chain is 8 retellings of about 150 words by two small open models taking turns, not the reader models: 3,840 texts.
ideas.method: Readers: Qwen3 8B, Llama 3.1 8B; presence rule set on tuning stories. A gain is a unit absent from the seed and from the story's first retellings, present at step 8, and rare elsewhere (not house style). Copied: also in the chain's own step 4, in no sibling. Rebuilt: in a sibling's step 8. Null: chain labels shuffled within story.
ideas.rivals: The same count on content words and on LLM-listed plot points; sentence embeddings, text length, random units and the mean-pooled residual stream for the matching test only. The LLM plot-point list is most dangerous. The ratio is a result about transmission whichever tool gives it; units earn a place only if a human check of 200 gains favours them.
ideas.premise: P1. Also bears on how E2 is read. A ratio above 2 answers Sperber for these tellers. A ratio below 1 means resemblance in retold culture is largely convergence, so a neuron-defined meme would measure a shared attractor and not a lineage.
ideas.bio: Parallel evolution in replicate lines, against inherited mutations
ideas.cost: M. About 3,900 short texts from local 4-bit models, one to two days of laptop time, plus two reading passes and one LLM plot-point pass.
ideas.payoff: A number for how much of what a retold story gains is inherited and how much is rebuilt, plus a list of convergent units to exclude from later lineage tests.
ideas.risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and the retelling prompt sets how faithfully they copy, so the ratio is a fact about these tellers. Small models may add little, leaving too few gains. Dropped details are not counted, because selection and attraction predict the same losses.
ideas.review: The original ratio depended on how profiles were centred and counted house style as attraction. Replaced with six replicate chains per story and a count of inherited gains against gains that recur in sibling chains. Remaining: model tellers, a prompt that sets fidelity, and no human chains yet.

ideas.title: Silent and loud mutations in copied news quotes
ideas.question: When a news quote changes by one word as it is copied, can neuron units tell meaning-keeping changes from meaning-changing ones, and are the meaning-changing versions reused less often?
ideas.hypothesis: On 600 hand-labelled natural swaps, the change in pre-chosen units separates silent swaps (meaning kept) from loud ones (meaning changed) with an AUC of at least 0.75 (0.5 is chance), within 0.05 of sentence-embedding similarity. Loud versions are then reused by another site at most 80% as often as silent ones.
ideas.falsifier: AUC under 0.65, or more than 0.05 below embeddings (standard error about 0.02). For spread: with at least 3,000 swaps, 500 of them loud, a loud-to-silent reuse ratio above 0.95 whose 95% interval excludes 0.8. With fewer swaps the spread test is declared uninformative, not passed.
ideas.data: MemeTracker phrase clusters (SNAP; one 220 MB file, reachable 2026-11-08; August 2008 to April 2009; no licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived numbers). One-word swaps mined with Lerique and Roth's method (code GPLv3); the number of swaps is unknown until mined. 800 swaps labelled by hand, 150 of them twice. Tuning pairs built from WordNet synonyms and antonyms.
ideas.method: Pairs share every word but one, so word overlap cannot separate them. Drop tense, number and spelling changes. Choose units on built pairs (synonym swap silent, antonym swap loud) and 200 labelled swaps; score on 600. The best tool labels all swaps; compare reuse by a later, different site within parent quote and week. Null: labels shuffled within parent.
ideas.rivals: Edit distance (constant by design), WordNet synonymy and word-vector similarity of the two swapped words, sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM judging both versions, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM judge is most likely to win. The silent-to-loud split and the spread test then run on its labels and still give memetics a fidelity figure.
ideas.premise: P1. A pass shows units respond to meaning in natural minimal pairs, where the study had 31 hand-made rewordings. A fail says units are too coarse for short texts. The spread result says whether meaning is protected in copying; Atran and the memeticists both expect that, so it does not separate them.
ideas.bio: Synonymous against non-synonymous mutation (dN/dS)
ideas.cost: M. Model time is under a day because quotes are short; mining the swaps and hand-labelling 800 pairs take about three days for one person.
ideas.payoff: A first copying-fidelity figure for ideas as opposed to strings: what share of copying errors is silent, and whether meaning-changing errors are weeded out.
ideas.risk: Most MemeTracker variants are truncations, so clean one-word swaps may number only a few thousand. Which version is the parent is inferred from timing, not documented. A loud change may be the correction of a misquote, which would spread more and hide selection.
ideas.review: Replaced PAWS (word-order pairs, the wrong kind) with built synonym and antonym swaps; changed the spread outcome to reuse by another site and said when it is uninformative. Remaining: an LLM judge will win the labelling, swap counts are unknown, and parent direction is inferred.

ideas.title: Heylighen's selection criteria on randomised headline tests
ideas.question: Do the criteria that Heylighen (1998) says help a meme get noticed and accepted, scored by neuron units chosen in advance, predict which headline wins a randomised test?
ideas.hypothesis: On confirmatory tests, at least 4 of 6 criteria (distinctiveness, novelty, simplicity, authority, formality, utility) raise click rate with 95% intervals excluding zero, and together they add at least 2 points of winner accuracy over headline length and punctuation.
ideas.falsifier: Fewer than 3 of 6 criteria significant in the predicted direction, or under 1 added point, on at least 5,000 confirmatory tests where only the headline differs (standard error about 0.7 points). Separately, units fail if LLM ratings of the same criteria beat them by more than 1 point.
ideas.data: Upworthy Research Archive (OSF jd64p, CC BY 4.0): 32,487 randomised tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015. Drop tests the archive's own column flags for unreliable randomisation (about 22%); keep tests where only the headline differs (count not yet checked). Tune on its exploratory part, score once on its confirmatory part. Archived data; nothing is optimised on a live audience.
ideas.method: Use only criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation (being noticed, understood, accepted), which a click measures. For each, write 80 contrast pairs (same content, criterion high or low); pick units on 60, check on 20, freeze. No click data chooses units. Within each test, criterion differences predict the winner (conditional logistic regression), controlling length and punctuation. Null: arms shuffled within test.
ideas.rivals: An LLM rating each headline 1 to 7 on each criterion, readability and word-rarity formulas, an embedding probe trained on the contrast pairs, word n-grams, sparse-autoencoder features (Movva et al. 2025), random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM rater is most dangerous, because the criteria are defined in words. If it wins, the criteria still get a signed test.
ideas.premise: P1. If unit-scored criteria predict as well as LLM ratings, units measure abstract properties of a meme and not only words. If only the ratings work, the theory survives without the unit. If neither works, the criteria fail at the attention stage.
ideas.bio: Selection gradients on named traits
ideas.cost: M. 150,000 headlines take an hour or two per model; rating six criteria with a local LLM takes about a day.
ideas.payoff: The first test of Heylighen's assimilation criteria as a signed set on randomised data, and a check of whether units chosen in advance can stand in for a reader's rating.
ideas.risk: Simplicity is already known to win on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024), so one criterion is a replication. Heylighen himself hedges on formality. Contrast pairs written by an LLM may differ in style as well as in the criterion. Click-bait habits may swamp the rest.
ideas.review: Cut to the six criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation; expressivity and proselytism belong to later stages. Removed an unsourced count of flagged tests. Simplicity is already published on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024). Remaining: LLM ratings will probably tie the units.

ideas.title: Do reposted ideas wear out beyond their words
ideas.question: When an image is reposted to Reddit under a new title, does repeating the idea of an earlier title cost votes even when no words are shared?
ideas.hypothesis: Among reposts sharing no content word with earlier titles of the image, similarity in units to earlier titles lowers vote rank by at least 1.5 percentile points more (most against least similar third) than similarity to later titles, which cannot cause fatigue. The penalty is larger when the earlier post was in the same subreddit.
ideas.falsifier: An earlier-minus-later gap under 0.5 points, or of the wrong sign, on at least 20,000 reposts that have both earlier and later titles (standard error about 0.6 points, resampled by image). Units also fail if the gap disappears once sentence-embedding similarity is added to the model.
ideas.data: SNAP Reddit submissions (Lakkaraju et al. 2013): 132,308 posts of 16,736 images, July 2008 to January 2013, one 7.6 MB CSV. Counted on the file on 2026-11-08: 53,515 reposts share no content word with any earlier title, and 46,201 of those also have a later title. No licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived features.
ideas.method: First re-derive the published word-based title effect; units must reproduce it on reposts that share words. Outcome: vote rank within subreddit and month, adjusted for hour, repost number and days since the last post (a content-free baseline, after Weng). Predictor: similarity to earlier titles, and to later titles as placebo, in units, words and embeddings. Tune on 30% of images.
ideas.rivals: Word overlap (zero by design), sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM asked whether two titles make the same point, title length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. Embeddings are most dangerous. If they win, idea fatigue is still shown beyond words, which is Coscia's claim under control, and the unit is not needed for it.
ideas.premise: P1. A penalty that units detect where words cannot would show units following a short idea through rewording in wild data. A null or an embedding tie leaves P1 where Batman left it.
ideas.bio: Negative frequency-dependent selection
ideas.cost: S. 132,000 short titles, under an hour per model, and a day of analysis.
ideas.payoff: Whether competition for attention acts on ideas or on strings, and an answer to whether similar memes help or hurt each other with the content held fixed.
ideas.risk: Titles are short (median 5 words, counted on the file) and describe an image the model never sees, so unit profiles may be mostly noise. A title close to earlier ones may only be a plain description; the later-title placebo removes that only if plain titles are as common early as late.
ideas.review: Made the later-title placebo the test statistic and added a same-subreddit contrast, because closeness to earlier titles may only mark a plain description. Confirmed 53,515 eligible reposts on the file. Remaining: titles have a median of 5 words, so unit profiles may be noise.

ideas.title: Do memes survive retelling better in bundles
ideas.question: Does a story element survive a chain of retellings more often when its usual partner element (say, a vow of revenge beside an orphaned hero) is in the story than when an unrelated element takes the partner's place?
ideas.hypothesis: After four retellings an element survives at least 10 percentage points more often in a whole bundle than in a broken one, the gap is positive in at least 17 of 24 bundles, and a neutral filler element shows less than half that gap.
ideas.falsifier: A gap under 3 points, or a 95% interval (resampled by bundle) that includes zero, over 1,440 chains from 480 seed stories (standard error about 3.5 points). That would mean elements are lost one by one, and the memeplex adds nothing to its parts in transmission.
ideas.data: Built for the test. 24 two-element bundles fixed in advance, from the trope pairs that co-occur most in the TV Tropes tables of Gala et al. 2020 (pair list only; the site's licence is non-commercial). Each gets 10 outlines, written whole and broken: 480 name-free 300-word stories, 3 chains of 4 retellings, 5,760 texts. Released with its lineage.
ideas.method: A memeplex is a set of memes said to help each other spread. A coin flip decides whether the partner is present, so topic cannot explain the gap. Survival at the last step is read by units chosen on separate planted-element stories and checked against 400 human-labelled retellings. Statistic: survival in whole minus broken stories, paired by outline.
ideas.rivals: A keyword list for each element, an embedding probe, an LLM reader asked whether the element is present, text length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM reader is most dangerous, and the keyword list will win for elements with an obvious word. If either wins, the bundle effect is still the first randomised test of co-adapted memes.
ideas.premise: P1. The bundle effect itself does not depend on the unit. Units earn a place only if units chosen on planted stories track an element through four rewordings as accurately as the LLM reader, judged against the human labels.
ideas.bio: Fitness epistasis; co-adapted gene complexes
ideas.cost: M. About 6,500 short texts from local 4-bit models, two to three days of laptop time, plus half a day labelling 400 retellings.
ideas.payoff: A causal number for whether memes in a complex protect each other in transmission, and a list of bundles that behave as larger units.
ideas.risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and four short retellings may keep everything (chain length is set on tuning stories). Memory research already shows that causally linked events are recalled better (Trabasso and van den Broek 1985), so a pass may be old news under a new name.
ideas.review: The citation version could not fail: units that co-fire inside the model, and words in set phrases, stay linked whatever culture does. Rewritten as a randomised test of whether a partner element protects an element in retelling. Remaining: model tellers; memory research partly predicts the result.

ideas.title: Know Your Meme family tree
ideas.question: Does a meme entry carry the units of its documented parent meme more than those of unrelated memes?
ideas.note: IMKG (Tommasini et al. 2023) and the Zannettou et al. 2018 Zenodo set hold the links. Hosting, licence and scraping terms are unchecked. Captions follow templates, so word overlap will probably win; the images need vision neurons.

ideas.title: Dennett's grain size
ideas.question: At what unit size (single neuron, merged family, sentence, document) does heredity along citations peak, and does the curve differ from the one for unigram, bigram and phrase?
ideas.note: Reuses ME21's data. A flat curve, or one that tracks the n-gram curve, means there is no natural meme size.

ideas.title: Edmonds' Challenge 1, items 4 and 5
ideas.question: Do unit frequencies across generations of papers show a non-zero selection term in a Price-equation split, against a content-free limited-attention simulation?
ideas.note: Weng et al. 2012 supplies the null; the rival is the same split on n-grams. Analysis only once ME21 exists.

ideas.title: The 1997 learned unit, side by side
ideas.question: Do Pocklington and Best's latent-semantic term clusters match neuron units on ME21's word-matched citation test?
ideas.note: A learned unit was tried 29 years ago and changed nothing. If it ties neurons here, the instrument was not what memetics lacked.

ideas.title: Memorable against forgotten movie lines
ideas.question: Do Heylighen's criteria, scored by the units frozen in ME24, pick the memorable quote over a matched line by the same speaker in the same scene?
ideas.note: Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. 2012. The Cornell data page failed with a certificate error again on 2026-11-08, so hosting is unconfirmed. The rival is their word-rarity model. It would cover the retention stage, which ME24 cannot.

ideas.title: Lynch's pass-it-on unit
ideas.question: Is there a unit for 'urge the reader to pass this on', and does it predict copy number in chain letters or copy-pasted posts?
ideas.note: No public cascade data found: Adamic et al.'s Facebook data is closed and the chain-letter archive was unreachable. A keyword list is the rival and will be hard to beat.

ideas.title: Sperber's test on human chains
ideas.question: Does ME22's copied-to-rebuilt ratio hold when people do the retelling, and how much of what survives is explained by the receiver and not the source (Gabora)?
ideas.note: Breithaupt et al. 2018 ran 285 human chains of three retellings, but on only three base stories, and whether the retelling texts are public is unconfirmed (one supplementary file). Needed before ME22 says anything about people.

ideas.title: Copy the product or the instructions
ideas.question: Do chains that regenerate a story from an outline keep more units than chains that paraphrase the finished text, as Blackmore claims?
ideas.note: Blackmore's distinction is confirmed; which mode she ranks as more faithful is from memory. Rival: content-word retention. A cheap extra arm for ME22.

ideas.title: Linkage along citations (was ME26)
ideas.question: Are pairs of units passed from a cited paper to a citing paper together more often than their separate rates predict?
ideas.note: Demoted. Units that co-fire inside the model and words in set phrases would stay linked across periods whatever culture does, and a shared subtopic gives the same pattern. It needs pairs with no background association before it can fail.

ideas.title: A mutation rate per retelling
ideas.question: What share of units is lost or gained at each step of a retelling chain, and is the rate lower for units than for content words?
ideas.note: Free once ME22's chains exist. Dawkins's copying fidelity as a number. The rival is the same rate on words and on LLM-listed plot points; a figure for people needs the human chains named in the Sperber seed.

ideas.title: Citations the paper leans on
ideas.question: Does ME21's unit advantage grow for references that the citing paper mentions several times in its full text?
ideas.note: Answers ME21's weak ground truth with a dose measure that does not come from the abstracts. Needs open full text with in-text citation counts (the PubMed Central open-access subset that Kuhn used); parsing and coverage are unchecked.

ideas.title: Prior-art search still owed
ideas.question: Has anyone already used neuron or sparse-autoencoder features as the unit in a citation, headline or retelling-chain test?
ideas.note: Web search was unavailable during this review (the shared budget was used up), so checks were limited to dataset pages, Crossref and the arXiv API. Run a proper search before any design here is expanded.

ideas.title: Is everything a remix? A ledger with a floor
ideas.question: Once measurement noise is removed, what share of a film plot's meme units and unit pairs had never appeared in any earlier plot, and is that more than chance once release dates are shuffled?
ideas.hypothesis: Remix nearly holds. Under 1% of a late film's repeatable units are first appearances. Yet new memes exist: recurring units born after 2000 number at least twice the count found when release years are shuffled. New pairings of old units exceed their shuffled count by at least 1.5 times.
ideas.falsifier: Unit birth excess under 1.2 with a bootstrap interval including 1: no detectable invention, or a blind instrument. First-appearance share over 5%: remix fails. Stop early if two-summary agreement (kappa) is under 0.4 or within 0.1 of mismatched films. Check on 1985 to 1999 births that at least 200 born units exist.
ideas.data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 plot summaries of 29,505 stories from five Wikipedia language editions, machine-translated to English, with Wikidata year and genre. Sample 8,000 films with two or more summaries. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA; the dataset's own licence is unconfirmed. About 13% of summary pairs are direct translations; drop near-duplicates.
ideas.method: Set each unit's presence bar on 1,500 unscored films. A unit is in a film only if present in two differently worded summaries. Count units and pairs seen in two or more films whose first appearance falls after 2000. Null: release years permuted within genre and length band. Statistic: observed-to-shuffled ratio (birth excess), bootstrapped over films.
ideas.rivals: The same ledger with word stems and stem pairs, Llama Scope sparse-autoencoder features, random non-meme units and embedding clusters; a reconstruction score (Lu 2025); an LLM listing what is new (500 films); length. Most dangerous: word stems, since new things bring new words. If stems give the same excess, the finding stands without neurons.
ideas.premise: P1. If presence does not repeat across two wordings better than word stems do, neuron novelty scores are uninterpretable and the unit adds nothing here. Running Qwen and Llama shows whether two models call the same units new, a first P2 check for novelty.
ideas.bio: De novo genes versus duplication and recombination.
ideas.cost: M: about a week. Roughly 20,000 summaries, a few hours of forward passes per model; the permuted ledger over unit pairs is the heavy computation.
ideas.payoff: A version of 'everything is a remix' that can fail, with numbers for inherited, new and newly combined; and the first test-retest reliability figure for meme presence, which every novelty measure depends on.
ideas.risk: Summaries in different language editions may share a source, inflating repeatability. A unit seen once cannot be told from noise, so only recurring units count. With 8,000 films, 'new' can still mean 'not sampled'. Birth excess shows time structure, which fashion cycles also produce.
ideas.review: The earlier-to-later ratio was 1 by identity (every unit has one first and one last appearance); replaced by a date-shuffle null on recurring units. Tell Me Again now supplies every film. Remaining: dataset licence unconfirmed; the two summaries are not fully independent.

ideas.title: Undeclared influence, checked against the written record
ideas.question: Can a method tuned on declared 'based on' and 'inspired by' links find influence between works that Wikidata does not declare but the written record confirms?
ideas.hypothesis: On held-out loose links ('inspired by', 'references work'), neurons rank the true source in the top 5% of matched decoys at least 5 points more often than the best cheap rival. At least 10% of their top 1,000 undeclared pairs are confirmed by the record, against under 2% for random matched pairs.
ideas.falsifier: Loose-link advantage under 2 points, or its 95% interval includes zero (1,000 pairs give a standard error near 2 points; do not run with under 500). Or the confirmed share of the top 1,000 is no higher than the best rival's. After E2, a second failure would settle that neurons add nothing to words for tracing influence.
ideas.data: Wikidata links with English Wikipedia articles at both ends, counted 2026-11-08, CC0: based on (P144) 30,685; inspired by (P941) 3,713; references work (P8371) 1,239. Plot sections, CC BY-SA, names masked. Sample 6,000 pairs with plots at both ends, loose links oversampled: 2,000 for development, 4,000 held out. Non-plot article text is the documentary record.
ideas.method: Score pairs by hub-adjusted share of the source's rare units (the E2 statistic). Test 1: rank held-out true sources among decoys matched on decade, medium and genre, per link type. Test 2: for each method's top 1,000 unlinked pairs with different creators and series, an LLM auditor must quote the article sentence naming the source (200 hand-checked). Null: within-decade permutation.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and BM25 on the same masked plots; e5 sentence embeddings and story-emb, which was built to survive name replacement; an LLM reading both plots (shortlists only); text length; random non-meme units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: story-emb and the LLM. If they win, undeclared-influence search still works, just without neurons.
ideas.premise: P1. A pass is the first evidence that neuron units trace influence where plots are not simply retold. A fail leaves P1 with no practical content for descent. For P2, report how many of the top 1,000 pairs Qwen and Llama share, against the random-unit floor.
ideas.bio: Detecting horizontal gene transfer, validated on known transfers.
ideas.cost: M: about two weeks. Roughly 20,000 plots, a few hours of forward passes per model; the LLM reader on shortlists, the auditor on about 5,000 pairs and a 200-pair hand check are the main cost.
ideas.payoff: A search tool for unacknowledged sources with a known hit rate, tested on thousands of works beyond one franchise; or a clear finding that embeddings already do the job.
ideas.risk: Similarity is not influence: top pairs may be genre twins, and critics note resemblance, so only statements that the makers drew on the source count. The record misses unwritten influence. Models may recognise famous plots despite masked names. Outputs are candidates, never accusations of copying.
ideas.review: Dropped the 'lowest quarter of word overlap' stratum: selecting on a rival's score makes that rival lose by construction. Strata are now link types. Audit made checkable and enlarged; same-franchise and same-creator pairs excluded. Remaining: the number of loose links with plots at both ends is unconfirmed.

ideas.title: Atypical meme pairings and clicks, topic held fixed
ideas.question: Within one randomised headline test, does the headline whose meme units are paired in ways rarely seen in earlier headlines win more clicks?
ideas.hypothesis: Yes, modestly. With test and image held fixed, one standard deviation more rare-pair atypicality raises click odds by at least 1%, after controls for length, words, word pairs and single neuron units. A squared term for an inverted U adds nothing detectable.
ideas.falsifier: The 95% interval for the rare-pair odds ratio lies wholly below 1.005, or includes 1 while word-pair atypicality passes. Robertson et al. 2023 resolved a 2.3% effect per negative word on these tests, so 1% should be detectable; confirm the standard error on the exploratory set before scoring.
ideas.data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 randomised headline tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015, CC BY 4.0, OSF node jd64p. Fit on the exploratory set (4,873 tests); score once on the confirmatory set (22,743). Drop the faulty-randomisation window (about 22%) and compare only arms sharing an image: roughly 9,000 usable confirmatory tests, to confirm.
ideas.method: Fix the 2,000 most frequent units on exploratory headlines. Score each unit pair in a headline by how often it co-occurred in earlier headlines against a shuffle keeping unit frequencies and month (Uzzi's z-score). Model clicks per impression with a fixed effect per test, adding feature sets in nested steps. Null: arms permuted within test.
ideas.rivals: Word-pair atypicality; single neuron units without pairs; TF-IDF difference; embedding distance from earlier headlines; an LLM asked which headline wins and which is more surprising; length and punctuation; random units; sparse-autoencoder features (Movva 2025). Most dangerous: word pairs, because headlines are short. If they win, recombination is tested anyway and neurons are surplus.
ideas.premise: Assumes both. A pass shows that pairs of neuron units carry combination structure that word pairs and a bag of single units miss. A fail while word pairs pass says recombination matters but this unit does not. Repeat in Llama to see if the pair scores agree.
ideas.bio: Epistasis: the fitness of gene combinations beyond single genes.
ideas.cost: S: under 2 days. 150,817 headlines is about 40 minutes of forward passes per model on the pre-registration's timing, which is optimistic; the LLM rival on a subsample is the dearest part.
ideas.payoff: A topic-controlled test of 'familiar base plus one surprise' (Uzzi; Berlyne's inverted U), and a pair-novelty score that could be used when drafting.
ideas.risk: A headline holds too few units for pair statistics to mean much. Novelty is not randomised, only the audience is, so atypical headlines may differ in other ways. Sparse-autoencoder features have already been applied to this archive, so the ground is not new.
ideas.review: Arms also vary the image, so compared arms must share it; usable tests fall from 17,700 to about 9,000. Switched from winner-picking accuracy to within-test click odds for power. Added single units as a baseline that pairs must beat. Remaining: the effect is probably tiny.

ideas.title: A writer's imprint across a language border
ideas.question: Do an author's distinctive units reappear in documented followers who wrote in another language, where shared words and function-word style cannot carry the signal?
ideas.hypothesis: Neurons place the documented influencer in the top 3 of 21 candidate authors for at least 30% of pairs (chance is 14%), at least 5 points more often than the best multilingual embedding and than always guessing the most famous candidate.
ideas.falsifier: Top-3 rate under 20%, or no higher than multilingual embeddings, translate-then-TF-IDF or the fame-only guess. 300 pairs give a standard error near 2.7 points: ample against chance, but only about 50% power for a 5-point gap over a rival, so a gap between 0 and 5 is undetermined. Do not run with under 250 pairs.
ideas.data: Wikidata 'influenced by' (P737): 32,322 statements, counted 2026-11-08, CC0. Pairs where both authors died before 1955, share no writing language and have Wikisource pages: 798 pairs, 364 followers. Only 166 such followers have Project Gutenberg author pages, so take texts from Wikisource dumps (public domain or CC BY-SA). Target 300 pairs, 20,000 words of prose per author, original language.
ideas.method: Choose each influencer's distinctive units on half of that author's text, against same-language authors of the same era. For each follower, rank the documented influencer among 20 decoys matched on language, era and fame (number of Wikipedia language editions) by how many of those units the follower's text carries. Statistic: top-3 rate, clustered by follower. Null: decoys permuted within era.
ideas.rivals: Multilingual sentence embeddings; machine translation to English, then TF-IDF and Burrows Delta (function-word stylometry); an LLM given both texts and the 21 names; always picking the most famous candidate; length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: the LLM, which may simply know that Baudelaire read Poe. Report obscure pairs separately to blunt that.
ideas.premise: Both. P1: a unit that survives a change of language is not a word detector. P2: Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 should rank the same influencers; report their agreement against the random-unit floor. A fail bounds 'a person's influence' to style and translation.
ideas.bio: Introgression: tracing one parent's alleles in a hybrid lineage.
ideas.cost: M: up to two weeks. About 600 authors at 20,000 words is a few hours of forward passes per model; assembling clean public-domain prose in several languages from Wikisource is the labour.
ideas.payoff: A per-person influence score that works across languages and is checked against documented influence; or a bound showing neurons add nothing to embeddings for it.
ideas.risk: Too few pairs survive the prose and length filters. P737 records fame as much as influence, and followers often read the influencer in translation. The models have probably memorised these classics, so units may recognise the texts instead of their content; the LLM reader shares that flaw.
ideas.review: Gutenberg yields only 166 qualifying followers, below the design's own floor, so texts now come from Wikisource (364 followers). Added fame-matched decoys and a fame-only rival, because P737 favours famous influencers. Remaining: Wikisource prose coverage per author is unchecked and the expected signal is weak.

ideas.title: Novelty and resonance over time, across two models
ideas.question: Do novelty, transience and resonance scores built from neuron units predict later citations beyond word-based versions, and do two models give the same scores?
ideas.hypothesis: Neuron resonance adds at least 0.01 AUC (ranking accuracy; 0.5 is chance) over TF-IDF, topic-model and embedding resonance together with venue and team size, and adds more with a 10-year forward window than with 3. After removing TF-IDF resonance, Qwen and Llama scores rank-correlate at least 0.1 above scores from random units.
ideas.falsifier: Added AUC under 0.005 with an interval including zero (15,000 test abstracts; paired standard error about 0.004, to confirm by bootstrap): no use beyond words. Or residual cross-model correlation no higher than for random non-meme units, which agree almost freely: the score carries nothing specific to memes.
ideas.data: OpenAlex (CC0; the API now needs a free key with a daily budget): about 45,000 abstracts from one field, 2000 to 2025, with reference lists, venue and citations counted to 2025. Abstracts average about 8 sentences. Years 2000 to 2007 fix units and settings; 2008 to 2015 are scored once; later years serve only as the future pool.
ideas.method: Novelty is an abstract's mean distance from abstracts of the previous 3 years; transience is its distance from the next 3 (or 10); resonance is novelty minus transience (Barron 2018). Predict top-10% citations within field and year with nested logistic models. Null: abstracts shuffled within year. Fields rename ideas, so word scores should fade with the longer window.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF backward and forward similarity (Kelly 2021); topic-model resonance (Barron 2018); sentence-embedding resonance; an LLM rating novelty from the abstract (subsample); abstract length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: TF-IDF, which already tracks patent quality. If it wins, resonance works and neurons are surplus; the cross-model figure still tests P2.
ideas.premise: Both. P1 gains only if the neuron score adds prediction where vocabulary has turned over. P2 gains if two models' scores agree beyond what shared words and random units explain; the study's one beyond-words result held in Llama and failed in Qwen.
ideas.bio: Fate of a new mutation: lost, transient or fixed in descendants.
ideas.cost: M: about 4 days. API pull of 45,000 abstracts, under two hours of forward passes per model, then regressions.
ideas.payoff: A model-independent influence score for any dated body of text, or a finding that the TF-IDF ratio is all one needs.
ideas.risk: Citations reward fame and venue, so every text measure adds little. Later papers cite what they resemble, so resonance partly restates citation. Resonance in a 3-year window rewards joining a trend as much as starting one.
ideas.review: The sample ended in 2015, leaving scored years without later abstracts; the pool now runs to 2025. The cross-model bar was an absolute 0.3, which random units would pass; it is now a margin over random units. Venue and team size added. Remaining: 'TF-IDF suffices' is the likely result.

ideas.title: Who or what: a Girard and Dawkins split
ideas.question: When a researcher is exposed to an idea new to them, is adoption explained more by which idea it is (Dawkins) or by who displayed it (Girard)?
ideas.hypothesis: Dawkins: an idea's adoption lift repeats across separate halves of exposers (r of 0.5 or more) and predicts held-out adoption better than the exposer's lift does. Girard: with the idea held fixed, one standard deviation more exposer prestige raises adoption odds by 20%. Our bet: Dawkins on both counts.
ideas.falsifier: Prestige odds ratio of 1.2 or more with an interval excluding 1, or exposer lift predicting held-out adoption as well as idea lift: a content-only account fails here. Idea split-half r under 0.2: ideas show no stable merit. Needs 5,000 exposers and 2,000 ideas with 20 or more offers each; confirm on development years.
ideas.data: OpenAlex (CC0; free API key): the RX25 field sample widened to about 60,000 abstracts, 2000 to 2020, with citation links and author identifiers. Prestige is an author's citations received inside the sample before the exposure year. A citation is the exposure record. Early years fix a dictionary of 3,000 repeatable units; later years are scored.
ideas.method: Event: B's authors cite A in year t; a unit in A, absent from their earlier abstracts and from B, is 'offered'. Outcome: it appears in their abstracts within 3 years. Lift is adoption over the unit's field-year base rate. Logistic model: fixed effect per unit, prestige and prior citer-to-cited similarity. Null: cited authors permuted within field and year.
ideas.rivals: The same analysis with keywords and noun phrases, embedding clusters and LLM-extracted claims (subsample) as the idea; exposure count alone; random units. Most dangerous: keywords, since in abstracts a new term is the idea. If keywords give the same answer, it stands without neurons. Wording does not confound the who-or-what split itself.
ideas.premise: Assumes both. Neuron memes measure only the 'what'. If who-effects dominate, a content-only science of memes misses most of the story however good the unit. If the answer changes with the unit type, the unit matters (P1).
ideas.bio: Strain fitness versus super-spreader hosts.
ideas.cost: M: one to two weeks. Pulling author histories is the labour; about 2 hours of forward passes per model; the models fit on a laptop with subsampling.
ideas.payoff: A head-to-head of the mimetic and memetic accounts on one dataset, which the literature search did not find, and a ceiling on what any content measure can explain.
ideas.risk: Citing is not random exposure: authors cite those they already resemble, and famous papers draw ceremonial citations that lower adoption, which biases against Girard. A citation does not prove reading. Girard's distinctive claims, rivalry and scapegoating, are not tested; this is prestige bias.
ideas.review: The outcome sat in the citing paper itself, so 'adoption' restated why it cited; it is now measured in later papers. The variance ratio reflected unit base rates and group sizes; replaced by split-half and held-out comparisons. Remaining: exposure is self-selected, so identification stays weak.

ideas.title: Planted influence with look-alike decoys
ideas.question: When a writer is shown a source and told to copy, transform or combine it, can neurons name that source once the wording no longer resembles it?
ideas.hypothesis: In the deep-transform condition (new setting, names and wording; content-word overlap with the source no higher than with look-alikes), neurons rank the true source first among 20 candidates for at least 40% of stories (chance is 5%), at least 10 points above the best embedding. For close copies every method is near ceiling.
ideas.falsifier: Deep-transform accuracy under 15%, or no higher than the best of story-emb, e5 and the LLM judge. 200 held-out stories per condition give a standard error near 3.5 points, enough to see a 10-point paired gap. Stories written with no source must put any candidate first at the 5% chance rate.
ideas.data: Built. 250 source plots of little-known films from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia plots, CC BY-SA). Each gets 19 look-alike decoys of the same genre, decade and length, never shown to the writer. Two LLM writers from families other than the readers produce 1,250 stories: copy, transform, deep transform, combine two sources, or no source.
ideas.method: Fix units and settings on 50 development sources; score 200 held out. Rank each story's candidates by the hub-adjusted share of the source's rare units (the E2 statistic). Statistic: top-1 accuracy by condition, plus second-source recall for combined stories. A script checks that word overlap falls across conditions. Null: source labels permuted within genre.
ideas.rivals: TF-IDF and BM25; e5 embeddings and story-emb; an LLM judge reading the story and its candidates; length; random units; mean-pooled residual stream. Most dangerous: story-emb and the LLM judge, both made to ignore surface wording. If they win, influence search works without neurons, and the depth of rewording at which each method fails is still new.
ideas.premise: P1. Truth is known by construction and wording is removed by design, so a pass is direct evidence that units carry inherited content beyond words. A fail leaves no setting where neurons trace influence better than cheap tools. For P2, compare Qwen and Llama rankings against random units.
ideas.bio: Experimental crosses with known parentage.
ideas.cost: S to M: about 3 days. 1,250 generated stories of about 400 words, minutes of forward passes per model; the LLM judge over 1,250 stories with 20 candidates each is the main cost.
ideas.payoff: The first test where influence is certain and wording cannot explain it; a curve of accuracy against depth of rewording for every method; and a calibration set for RX21 and RX22.
ideas.risk: Reader neurons may detect LLM writing habits instead of content; a small human-written arm would settle that and is not costed here. Instructed transformation may be easier to trace than real influence. Overlaps with the paused planted-story plan, which plants memes, not sources.
ideas.review: Added by the reviewer, promoted from the planted-influence seed: the area had no design where influence is known by construction. Weakness: writers and readers are both language models, so a human-written arm is needed before a pass is trusted.

ideas.title: Remix ledger calibrated on built remixes
ideas.question: If stories are assembled from known sources plus planted new elements and then reworded, does the measured inherited share track the true share?
ideas.note: The instrument check for RX21; RX27's combined stories can supply the material. Falsified if the neuron ledger's correlation with the planted proportions is no higher than a word n-gram ledger's. From l8 S3.

ideas.title: Naming the second parent
ideas.question: After removing a work's best single source, can a method name the second source of works documented to draw on two?
ideas.note: Blending, not branching, is the honest model for franchises. RX27 covers the built case; this is the real one, on documented multi-source films. Rivals: TF-IDF residuals and an LLM asked directly. From l6 seed 5.

ideas.title: Do rivals become doubles?
ideas.question: Do documented rivals (competing franchises, feuding authors) grow more alike in their units over time than matched non-rival pairs, as Girard predicts?
ideas.note: The part of Girard that RX26 leaves untested. Needs a defensible list of rivalries with dates; the rival measure is embedding convergence.

ideas.title: An author's imprint by construction
ideas.question: When an LLM writer is steeped in one public-domain author and writes on unrelated subjects, do neurons identify that author against decoys?
ideas.note: Expected to lose to function-word stylometry; worth running because it bounds what 'influence of a person' can mean for content units. Cheaper and cleaner than RX24. From l8 S6.

ideas.title: Descent or attractor
ideas.question: Can incidental 'hitchhiker' units separate pairs with documented descent from pairs documented as independent invention?
ideas.note: Answers Sperber's objection that shared traits need no line of descent. The lexical rival is rare shared words and named details. The labelled pairs are the work.

ideas.title: Declared remix trees
ideas.question: On a platform with declared parent links (Scratch, Thingiverse), how much of a remix is inherited from its parent, and does the parent's popularity or its content predict what is kept?
ideas.note: Declared links give exposure for free and would sharpen RX26. Data access and licences were not checked; Scratch projects are code, so text is thin.

ideas.title: Citations the author did not declare
ideas.question: Do neuron units link a patent to prior art that the examiner added but the applicant did not cite?
ideas.note: A possible real ground truth for undeclared influence. Alcacer and Gittelman 2006 (doi:10.1162/rest.88.4.774) is now confirmed; examiners add about 40% of citations. Patent text data and licence still to check; TF-IDF is the rival (Kelly 2021).

ideas.title: A chamber as shared exposure
ideas.question: When every member hears every speech, is the later uptake of a new unit predicted by who introduced it (leader, senior member) or by which unit it is?
ideas.note: Added in review. Fixes RX26's self-selected exposure. ParlSpeech V2: 6.3 million speeches, nine parliaments, date, speaker and party, CC0 (Harvard Dataverse, checked 2026-11-08). Confounds: party talking points and the agenda. Speaker rank must be joined from elsewhere. Rival unit: keywords.

ideas.title: Same idea, different author
ideas.question: When two teams publish the same discovery at the same time, does the more prominent team's wording spread further in later papers?
ideas.note: Added in review. Holds the 'what' fixed so only the 'who' varies, the cleanest Girard test found. Bikard 2020 lists simultaneous discoveries; Huber et al. 2022 randomised author prominence in peer review. Dataset access and size not checked. Rival: word and phrase adoption.

ideas.title: Steer the named memes: a causal label test
ideas.question: When a labelled meme unit is pushed up while the model writes, do blind judges recover its label, even with the meme's usual words banned?
ideas.hypothesis: At one fluent dose per unit, at least 8 of the 31 named Qwen3-8B units pass: judges choose the unit's own label, from 31 plus 'none', on at least half of 20 held-out openings. With the label's words banned from the output, at most 4 still pass, mostly story patterns such as the funeral and the secret identity.
ideas.falsifier: Fewer than 4 of 31 units pass, or no more pass than at the 99th percentile when labels are shuffled among the 31 units' texts: then the labels are not causal. More than 4 passes under the ban refutes the word-emitter half. Shuffled labels should give about one pass or fewer, so 31 units are enough.
ideas.data: No new corpus. The 31 unit labels fixed in October 2026 (`study/results/labels.json`, MIT). Ban lists fixed before generation: keywords from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, each unit's 20 most-promoted output words, and character names. 30 neutral story openings written for this test (10 to set doses, 20 held out). Qwen3-8B at 4-bit and 8-bit; Llama 3.1 8B twins as a replication.
ideas.method: Steering adds a fixed amount to one unit's activation as the model continues an opening. Each unit keeps the largest of five doses that leaves text at most three times as surprising as normal to the unsteered model. Two LLM judges, checked on 200 blind human ratings, choose a label. Secondary: switch the unit off and ask for the meme.
ideas.rivals: The unit's 20 most-promoted output words handed to the same judges with no generated text (most dangerous: if it ties, units emit names, confirming labels as words, not ideas). A prompt that asks for the label (ceiling). A direction built from keyword-matched sentences. 62 random units matched on layer and firing rate, showing how often any push draws a label.
ideas.premise: P1. Passes under the keyword ban are the first causal evidence that a unit carries an idea. Passes only without the ban mean units are word emitters. A general fail means the paper's labels describe what units read, not what they do.
ideas.bio: Gene overexpression: turn one gene up, look for the trait.
ideas.cost: S. One to two days on the laptop, a few dollars of judge calls, two hours of human rating.
ideas.payoff: The causal check the paper named as missing, for every showcase meme, and a shortlist of units safe to use as edit handles.
ideas.risk: In small 4-bit models the gap between no effect and gibberish is narrow, so many units may fail for dose reasons and the result reads as untested, not refuted.
ideas.review: Replaced the invented 5% null with a shuffled-label null, fixed one dose per unit on tuning openings, and fixed ban lists in advance. Remaining weakness: the file tags only 13 of the 31 labels as tropes; 8 are characters, which can hardly pass the ban.
sources: Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean

ideas.title: More A, less B: rewriting against prompting
ideas.question: Can any internal handle (one neuron, a direction or a sparse-autoencoder feature) move an existing story toward meme A and away from meme B better than simply asking a model to rewrite it?
ideas.hypothesis: No. The prompt-only rewrite gets the highest combined score, and the best internal handle reaches under 80% of it. Among handles, the difference-of-means direction (average activation on texts with the meme minus texts without) does best and the single neuron worst.
ideas.falsifier: The handle arm that scored best on the tuning stories, alone or added to the prompt, beats prompt-only by 0.05 or more on the 0-to-1 combined score, with a 95% interval above zero, on 160 held-out stories. That gives about 85% power if per-story differences have a spread of 0.2, less if meme pairs differ a lot.
ideas.data: 208 film plots from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia summaries, CC BY-SA), skipping the pre-registration's reserved films, cut to 10 sentences, names masked. For each of 16 seeded meme pairs from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`: 13 plots containing B and not A, confirmed by an LLM reader and a human (3 tuning, 10 held out). Llama Scope sparse autoencoders (Apache 2.0).
ideas.method: Six arms on Llama 3.1 8B: prompt only; one neuron; 20 neurons; direction; sparse-autoencoder feature (a unit from a separately trained dictionary of activations); prompt plus direction. Handles use EN-23's contrast sentences. A Qwen3-8B judge and blind humans score A up, B down, story kept and fluency, combined so that failing one sinks the score. Repeated with A's keywords banned.
ideas.rivals: Prompt-only rewriting, the most dangerous: it beat every activation method on AxBench. Also keyword insertion (paste A's typical words in), a random direction of equal size, and text length. If prompting wins, neurons stay meters and editing tools should be built on prompts scored by the instrument.
ideas.premise: P1. A handle that beats prompting shows units are causal levers on meaning, strong support. If prompting wins, P1 survives only as a way to read memes, and meme engineering means prompt and measure.
ideas.bio: Gene editing against selective breeding.
ideas.cost: M. About a week on the laptop, with PyTorch for the feature arm or a small rented GPU; judge calls; four hours of human rating.
ideas.payoff: A straight answer on whether to build a meme editor on activations or on prompts, and a benchmark for narrow story motifs, which AxBench does not cover.
ideas.risk: A prompt win is the expected result after AxBench, so the news value is modest. Judges may reward stated keywords, so arms look alike. The public sparse autoencoder was trained on the base model; if it rebuilds under 90% of the 4-bit Instruct model's activation variance, that arm is dropped.
ideas.review: The 1,000 random films are the paused pre-registration's held-out set, so the data moved to the CMU corpus. Base stories must now contain B, or 'less B' is empty. One pre-chosen handle contrast replaces five. Remaining weakness: a prompt win is already expected.
sources: Chen et al. 2025, Persona vectors, arXiv:2507.21509
He et al. 2024, Llama Scope, arXiv:2410.20526
Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013, CMU Movie Summary Corpus

ideas.title: Do reading units write?
ideas.question: Is the unit that best detects a meme in text also the unit that best produces it when pushed?
ideas.hypothesis: Mostly not. Across 20 memes, the 10 best detector units and the 10 best writer units share under 20% of their members, and detectors steer successfully less than half as often as writers.
ideas.falsifier: Detectors steer as well as writers (success rates within 10 points on held-out prompts), or the two top-10 sets overlap by more than 50%. Twenty memes give about 85% power for a 25-point gap if memes differ with a spread of 35 points. Detectors that steer no better than random units are sensors only.
ideas.data: 20 of the 34 meme definitions in `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`. For each, 60 LLM-written sentence pairs with and without the meme, its usual words banned, checked by a second model and a 10% human sample: 30 pairs to pick units, 30 held out. The study's own 18 mapped units (`preregistration/dev_units.json`). Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B open weights.
ideas.method: Detectors: units ranked by how well activation separates the pairs. Writers: 2,000 shortlisted units, each pushed on tuning prompts and ranked by the rise in probability of meme sentences. Steer the top 10 of each on 20 held-out prompts, keywords banned; a blind judge from the other model, human-checked, scores meme and coherence. Paired permutation test across memes.
ideas.rivals: Random same-layer units; a difference-of-means direction from the same pairs; a prompt asking for the meme (ceiling); a keyword list on the detection half. Most dangerous: the direction. If it both reads and writes while single units do one or neither, the meme is a direction, not a neuron.
ideas.premise: P1. If detectors do not write, 'which neurons fire' is a sensor reading and editing needs separately found units. If they do, one unit serves both, the strongest form of P1.
ideas.bio: Sensory against motor neurons.
ideas.cost: S to M. Three to five days on the laptop; the writer screen is forward passes only, a few hours.
ideas.payoff: A rule for choosing edit handles, and a verdict on whether the study's detector units can be reused for engineering at all. It also records whether writers detect, and whether a detector fires when the model is simply asked to write its meme.
ideas.risk: Writers are picked by the kind of push they are then tested on, so part of their lead over detectors is built in; the informative numbers are the overlap and detectors against random units. In 4-bit models the dose window may be too narrow for either set.
ideas.review: Writers were picked by gradient attribution, which Liu 2026 reports mispredicts control; now a direct push screen on tuning prompts. Added the keyword ban, a human check and the study's own 18 units. Remaining weakness: writers' lead is partly built in by how they are chosen.

ideas.title: Breeding captions on an archived fitness landscape
ideas.question: When a score-and-select loop may only move among captions that real people already rated, does scoring with model-internal units find funnier captions than scoring with embeddings or an LLM judge?
ideas.hypothesis: A tie. After 10 generations the unit-scored loop's final 20 captions sit within 3 percentile points of the embedding-scored loop's in real crowd rating, and both beat random selection by at least 5 points.
ideas.falsifier: The unit-scored loop ends more than 3 percentile points above or below the embedding-scored loop, with a 95% interval excluding zero across 100 held-out contests; a tie is claimed only if the whole interval sits within 3 points. Or no loop beats random selection by 5 points: caption text alone carries no breedable signal.
ideas.data: New Yorker caption contest rankings (Zhang et al. 2024; Hugging Face `yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking`): 365 contests, over 2.2 million captions, over 250 million crowd ratings, plus a text description of each cartoon. CC BY-NC 4.0, research use only: commit only IDs and scores. The earliest 265 contests train the scorers; the latest 100 are held out. Captions with under 25 ratings dropped.
ideas.method: Unit scorer: a linear model on Qwen3-8B units chosen on training contests. Every scorer sees the cartoon description. Gate: stop if no scorer picks a top-tenth caption over a bottom-half one 55% of the time in training. Runs start from 20 random captions; each generation offers every survivor's 5 nearest real captions by word overlap; the scorer keeps 20.
ideas.rivals: Scorers built on sentence embeddings (most dangerous: they tie fine-tuned models on headline data), TF-IDF, the mean-pooled residual stream, caption length, an LLM asked which caption is funnier, and random selection. Real ratings used as the scorer give the ceiling. A tie still leaves units able to name what selection favoured.
ideas.premise: Assumes both; tests P1 as a selection instrument. A win says internal units see appeal that embeddings miss. A tie leaves readable names as their only edge. A loss says breed with embeddings and use units only to describe the result.
ideas.bio: Directed evolution on a mapped fitness landscape (deep mutational scanning).
ideas.cost: M. About 10 hours of forward passes for every caption, or 3 on a sample; the LLM-judge arm is the slow part. One week.
ideas.payoff: The first test of meme breeding in which every candidate has a real human outcome, with no live audience and no persuasion.
ideas.risk: Text carries little of the joke. In Zhang et al. 2024, GPT-4 given a cartoon description picked a top-10 caption over one ranked near 1,000 only 65 to 67% of the time. All loops may hover near random and the gate may stop the study.
ideas.review: Added a go/no-go gate, the cartoon descriptions as input, a minimum rating count (the contest's bandit gives weak captions few ratings) and a proper rule for claiming a tie. Remaining weakness: nothing is generated, so this tests selection only, where text signal is weak.
sources: Zhang et al. 2024, Humor in AI, arXiv:2406.10522 (caption contest data)

ideas.title: What click-optimised breeding drifts toward
ideas.question: When a breeding loop selects headlines on a click predictor trained on real randomised tests, does it drift toward negativity and unsupported claims, and which brake holds it: a word list, named internal units or an LLM reviewer?
ideas.hypothesis: Against a random-selection loop, five generations of click selection raise negative words per headline by at least 50% and unsupported claims by at least 10 points. The word-list brake is evaded by rewording. The LLM reviewer holds judged negativity within 10% of the start while keeping 70% of the predicted click gain; the unit brake does no better.
ideas.falsifier: No drift beyond random selection (negative words up under 10%, unsupported claims up under 3 points); or the word list holds judged negativity as well as the reviewer; or the unit brake beats the reviewer (a safety use for units). 500 paired tests give about 90% power for a 3-point difference if per-test differences have a spread of 20 points.
ideas.data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 randomised headline tests, CC BY 4.0, OSF node jd64p. Drop the 22% of tests flagged for faulty randomisation and arms differing in image. Predictor and unit brake (10 named negativity and exaggeration units) fitted on the exploratory and confirmatory sets; 500 hold-out tests seed the loops. 300 headlines get blind human ratings.
ideas.method: Each loop starts from a test's losing headline. A local LLM, told only to rewrite, offers 8 variants per generation; the predictor selects. Unseen by the loop, drift is read by a negative-word count, a human-checked judge from another model family, and whether the test's own headlines and excerpt support each new claim. Arms: unbraked; three brakes; random selection.
ideas.rivals: Brakes: a negative-word list; an LLM reviewer asked whether a variant is more negative or less supported than the original (most dangerous, probably the best brake); a limit on embedding distance. Predictors: embeddings plus a linear model against unit profiles. The real gap between archived winners and losers is the yardstick for how much drift readers reward.
ideas.premise: Assumes both; tests a use. Because the optimiser rewords its way around word lists, this setting is built for units to beat words. If they still lose to the reviewer, P1 has no safety use here.
ideas.bio: Serial passage: selecting a pathogen for spread also selects for virulence.
ideas.cost: M. About 100,000 generated headlines and their forward passes, three days on the laptop, plus judge calls and two hours of human rating.
ideas.payoff: Measured limits for the programme's ethics rules: which brakes any optimiser must carry, and whether the instrument can enforce them. Nothing generated is shown to an audience.
ideas.risk: The click predictor is weak (about 46% at picking the winner among roughly three headlines), so drift may reflect its quirks, not what readers reward. El and Zou 2025 already showed this kind of drift with simulated audiences, so the new part is the comparison of brakes.
ideas.review: Drift is now measured against a random-selection loop, because LLM rewriting drifts unaided; the judge differs from the reviewer and is checked by humans; the hypothesis no longer contradicts its falsifier. Remaining weakness: selection is on predicted, not real, clicks.
sources: Matias et al. 2021, Upworthy Research Archive, doi:10.1038/s41597-021-00934-7
Robertson et al. 2023, Negativity drives online news consumption
El and Zou 2025, Moloch's Bargain, arXiv:2510.06105

ideas.title: Knock one motif out of the weights
ideas.question: Can a small edit to a model's weights stop it writing one story motif, including in paraphrase, with less side damage than a system prompt or a word ban?
ideas.hypothesis: Removing one direction from under 0.1% of the weights halves the motif's rate in free story writing, but a system prompt forbidding the motif leaves the rate at least 10 points lower still, with no more loss of story quality, averaged over 12 motifs. Switching off the motif's 10 best detector units changes nothing.
ideas.falsifier: Averaged over motifs, the weight edit leaves the motif rate at least 10 points below the prompt's at equal or smaller quality loss, with a 95% interval above zero. Or the edit fails outright: a fall of under 20%, no better than random directions. Twelve motifs give about 75% power if motifs differ with a spread of 12 points.
ideas.data: Apache 2.0 weights: Qwen3.5-0.8B (the model edited in the MIT post), Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B (the study's models). 12 motifs from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, kept only if the unedited model writes them on at least 40% of tuning prompts. Per motif, 300 LLM-written story prompts that invite it without naming it (100 to find the direction, 200 held out) and 100 unrelated prompts.
ideas.method: Direction: mean activation difference between stories with and without the motif, subtracted from the output weights of two layers, as in the MIT post. On 4-bit Qwen3-8B it is applied at run time. A second arm zeroes the motif's 10 best detector units. A blind, human-checked judge from another model family scores the motif as an idea, not a word.
ideas.rivals: A system prompt forbidding the motif (most dangerous: prompts and filters matched fine-tuning for forgetting concepts in Thaker et al. 2024). A ban on the motif's keywords, which should leave paraphrases. A fine-tune on motif-free stories. 20 random directions. If the prompt wins, weight edits are a curiosity, but the paraphrase result still shows whether an idea has a location.
ideas.premise: P1 in its direction form. A clean knockout shows a motif has a compact causal home in the weights. A fail means motifs are spread out or rebuilt elsewhere, so 'the meme is a unit' holds for reading at most.
ideas.bio: Gene knockout.
ideas.cost: M. One to two weeks on the laptop, plus judge calls. An agent-found edit, as in the MIT post, would be L.
ideas.payoff: Meme-free and meme-dosed model variants to use as control writers for planted-story tests, and a first check of weight-space editing on meaning.
ideas.risk: Sub-2B models write weak stories and may ignore a 'do not' instruction, so the prompt could lose for a reason that vanishes at 8B; the 8B run decides. The MIT authors found edits remove obstacles and cannot add abilities.
ideas.review: The '6 of 10 motifs' rule could not tell a win from a coin flip; replaced by a mean difference across 12 motifs. Added an 8B run, a base-rate gate and a detector-unit knockout arm. Remaining weakness: the prompt is expected to win, as in work on making models forget.
sources: Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab 2026, Sparks of weight-space programming
Thaker et al. 2024, Guardrail baselines for unlearning, arXiv:2403.03329

ideas.title: Is the unit needed to read the meme?
ideas.question: When a meme's detector units are switched off, does the model get worse at saying whether a passage contains that meme, and only that meme?
ideas.hypothesis: No. Switching off a meme's 10 best detector units lowers the model's yes-or-no accuracy on that meme by under 3 points, the same as matched random units. Removing the meme's difference-of-means direction (average activation with the meme minus without) lowers it by at least 10 points, and other memes' accuracy by under 3.
ideas.falsifier: Switching off the 10 units lowers accuracy on their own meme by 5 points or more beyond both matched random units and other memes' questions, with a 95% interval above zero. Twenty memes detect a 5-point drop with about 75% power if memes differ with a spread of 8 points.
ideas.data: EN-23's material: 20 memes from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, each with 60 LLM-written passage pairs with and without the meme, its usual words banned, checked by a second model and a 10% human sample; 30 pairs pick units, 30 are held out. The study's own 18 mapped units (`preregistration/dev_units.json`). Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B open weights.
ideas.method: The model reads a held-out passage and answers 'does this contain [definition]?' while the units are held at their average value on neutral text. Outcome: the fall in accuracy, and in confidence in the right answer, against the unharmed model. Own meme against other memes, paired permutation test across memes. Null: random units matched on layer and firing rate.
ideas.rivals: Removing the meme's difference-of-means direction (most dangerous: if it blinds the model while units do not, the meme is a direction). Switching off units that detect the meme's keywords. Matched random units. As a ceiling, deleting the meme's sentence from the passage. A null still tells us detector units are gauges beside the computation, not parts of it.
ideas.premise: P1. If the model reads the meme just as well without its detector units, they are correlates, and 'the meme is which neurons fire' holds as a measurement only. A specific loss would be the first evidence that the units are part of how the model understands the idea.
ideas.bio: Lesion study: remove one brain area, test one skill.
ideas.cost: S. One day on the laptop once EN-23's passages exist: forward passes only, no text generation, no paid judges.
ideas.payoff: The causal check from the reading side: whether the instrument's units are used by the model or merely move with the meme. It decides whether later work should track units or directions.
ideas.risk: Redundancy. Models often have several routes to an answer, so a null may mean back-up routes, not irrelevant units. The 2026 census found that silencing a neuron moves a model about a thousand times less than pushing it. The question may also be too easy or too hard for a 4-bit 8B model.
ideas.review: Added by the reviewer: the area steered units but never tested whether detector units are needed for reading. Remaining weakness: a null is ambiguous because of redundancy, and the areas on neurons as units or measurement validity may register a similar lesion test.
sources: Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean

ideas.title: Calibrate the judges first
ideas.question: Do the LLM judges used across these designs agree with blind human raters on whether a narrow motif is present when its usual words are banned?
ideas.note: Added by the reviewer; a shared prerequisite for every LLM-judged design here. About 600 short passages, from EN-23's material and from steered output, rated by two people and by each judge model. Rivals: a keyword check and an embedding probe. If judges agree with people much less than people agree with each other, enlarge the human samples.

ideas.title: Dose-window census of meme units
ideas.question: What share of the study's meme units have any dose that changes the text and keeps it fluent, compared with non-meme units matched on how word-like they are?
ideas.note: 500 meme and 500 matched units in Qwen3-8B. A 2026 census of Qwen3.5-4B (Öztürk, Research Square rs-11577020) confirmed 130 consistent neurons and reported that at least 6% of random pushes give a nameable, coherent change. Rivals: word-matched units and random directions. About one GPU-day.

ideas.title: Does 4-bit quantisation change steering?
ideas.question: Do dose windows and steering success differ between 4-bit, 8-bit and full-precision copies of the same model?
ideas.note: HedwigAI saw one neuron break the model at full precision but not at 8-bit; the study used 4-bit throughout. Cheap: rerun EN-21's best 10 units at three precisions (8-bit MLX builds of both study models exist). Decides whether laptop results transfer.

ideas.title: Write in Qwen, read in Llama
ideas.question: Does a meme written into text by steering Qwen with its keywords banned get picked up by Llama's twin unit better than by word-matched units, word overlap or an LLM reader?
ideas.note: Tests P2 through an intervention, not a correlation. Expect a null: the study's twin pairs fall to r = 0.14 on name-free text (`study/README.md`). Also a second way to make planted-meme stories for the paused pre-registration, with ground truth set by the push. About three days; depends on EN-21 finding handles that survive the ban.

ideas.title: Carry an edit across models
ideas.question: Does a meme direction found in Llama still write the meme after a learned map carries it into Qwen?
ideas.note: Oozeer et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.04429) report this for refusal and backdoor-removal steering vectors. Rivals: finding the direction afresh in Qwen, a map fitted on word-matched units, and plain prompting. No verified result yet for narrow story motifs.

ideas.title: A dial, not a switch
