ideas.question: Can a handle set how much of a meme a text carries in graded steps more reliably than prompt wording such as 'slightly more' or 'much more'?
ideas.note: Graded control is the one place steering might beat prompting. Outcome: blind judges rank five dose levels; score rank agreement. Rivals: prompt adverbs, and the number of meme sentences requested. Could run on EN-22's stories at little extra cost.

ideas.title: Do meme handles add up?
ideas.question: When two memes are pushed at once, do both appear in the text, or does one swamp the other?
ideas.note: A test of whether meme complexes can be assembled from parts. Rival: a prompt asking for both memes, and keyword insertion. Judge each meme separately and blind. Depends on EN-21 finding at least a few working handles.

ideas.title: Does breeding from the loser head toward the winner?
ideas.question: When a loop rewrites an Upworthy test's losing headline for several generations, do its outputs come to resemble the real winning headline more than the other real losers?
ideas.note: Added by the reviewer: an archived-outcome check on a loop that writes new text, which EN-24 cannot give. Arms differ only in the scorer (units, embeddings, LLM, random); blind judges say which real headline each output is closer to. Weak proxy: arms of one test share most words. Another archived mutation set: Humicroedit (Hossain et al. 2019, arXiv:1906.00274), 15,095 headline edits, mostly one word, rated for funniness.

ideas.title: Agent-found motif edit
ideas.question: Can an agent given a Python sandbox over a small model's weights find a cleaner motif knockout than the human recipe in EN-26?
ideas.note: Cost L: frontier-model agent time, as in the MIT weight-space post. Rivals: EN-26's direction removal, a system prompt, a keyword ban. Run only if EN-26 shows a knockout is possible at all.

ideas.title: Add one meme, ask real readers
ideas.question: When one meme is added to or removed from matched fiction premises, does reader preference move, and did any method forecast the direction?
ideas.note: Cost L. Needs an ethics note before registration: consented paid panel, fiction only, AI authorship disclosed, no targeting on personal traits, no raw-click outcome. Rivals: LLM-simulated readers, embeddings, human forecasters.

ideas.title: Most advanced yet acceptable: the headline novelty optimum
ideas.question: Within a randomised headline test, does the arm that is moderately new relative to recently published headlines win more clicks than very familiar or very new arms?
ideas.hypothesis: Click rate is an inverted U in novelty (an arm's distance from the site's previous 90 days of headlines). On confirmatory tests both slopes of a two-lines test are significant at 0.05, the peak falls between the 30th and 80th novelty percentiles, and the peak beats both extremes by at least 3% relative.
ideas.falsifier: On confirmatory tests no novelty measure shows a sign change at 0.05 (flat or monotonic), or the U is as strong against headlines from six months away (then it is house style, not familiarity). For neurons: adding neuron novelty to embedding and TF-IDF novelty gives no held-out likelihood gain (95% interval includes zero), overall and in the low-word-overlap subset.
ideas.data: Upworthy Research Archive (Matias et al. 2021): 32,487 tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015, CC BY 4.0, OSF jd64p. Fit on the exploratory split (4,873); score once on the confirmatory split (22,743). Drop tests flagged for the 2013 randomisation fault and arms differing in image: about 10,000 confirmatory tests should remain. Robertson et al. detected a 2.3% effect in 12,448.
ideas.method: Units: Qwen3-8B neuron families (neurons that fire together), chosen on exploratory data. Novelty: mean distance from an arm's unit profile to the prior 90 days' headlines. Arms compared within their own test, length controlled; two-lines test (one slope below a break point, one above). Null: novelty against a window six months away. Pre-set subset: arms sharing few stream words.
ideas.rivals: Novelty from TF-IDF backward similarity, sentence embeddings, the mean-pooled hidden state, sparse-autoencoder features on embeddings (a learned feature dictionary; Movva et al. 2025), an LLM rating 'how unusual for this site' against 20 recent headlines, headline length, random units. Embedding novelty is most dangerous: smooth and cheap. If it wins, the hunch is still tested causally; neurons add nothing.
ideas.premise: P1. A U found equally with words or embeddings settles the marketing claim and leaves P1 unmoved. A U that survives in the low-word-overlap subset for neuron novelty alone would show units track a familiar frame under new wording. Repeating it in Llama bears on P2.
ideas.bio: Optimal outbreeding: mates preferred slightly unlike kin.
ideas.cost: S. About 150,000 short headlines: under an hour of forward passes per model on the laptop. The LLM-rating rival runs on a 3,000-test subsample. No live audience; archived data only.
ideas.payoff: A causal answer to whether 'just past the familiar' wins, with the size of the effect and where the peak sits. If any measure works, a novelty ruler for planning creative tests.
ideas.risk: Arms of one test share a story, so their novelty may differ too little to trace a curve; the U then leans on comparing stories, which were not randomised. Upworthy effects are tiny, and Berger and Packard found a monotonic pattern for lyrics.
ideas.review: Replaced the within-month date shuffle, which barely moves a 90-day window, with a misplaced-window null; added headline length, the fault flag, the image rule and an estimated usable sample. Remaining weakness: novelty may vary little within a test. Prior-work check was arXiv only (nothing found); web search was unavailable.

ideas.title: Copied or coincidence: remakes against twin films
ideas.question: Do incidental 'hitchhiker' details shared by two similar films separate documented descent (remakes) from independent arrival at the same premise (twin films)?
ideas.hypothesis: With remake and twin pairs matched on overall likeness (sentence-embedding similarity), genre and length, a hitchhiker-sharing score separates them at AUC 0.70 or more (0.5 is chance) under two-fold cross-fitting (threshold set on one half of the pairs, scored on the other, then swapped), and neuron hitchhikers beat rare-word hitchhikers by at least 0.10 AUC.
ideas.falsifier: AUC below 0.60 for every hitchhiker definition: similarity cannot show descent in plot summaries. For neurons: AUC not above rare shared words (bootstrap interval of the difference includes zero). About 90 twin against 270 remake pairs gives a standard error near 0.035: enough to tell 0.70 from chance, and to see a neuron advantage only if it is about 0.10.
ideas.data: Wikipedia 'Twin films' list: 149 pairs (2026-11-08; CC BY-SA); about 110 after screening out shared sources and real events, perhaps 90 with usable plots. Remakes from Wikidata film-to-film 'based on' links (932 with both on English Wikipedia; CC0). Where available, the later film's plot comes from another-language Wikipedia, machine-translated (Tell Me Again, CC BY-SA 4.0). Names masked; dates withheld.
ideas.method: Hitchhiker: a unit shared by the pair but rare in the genre's other films (rarity set on films outside all pairs). Score: share of the earlier film's rare units found in the later one, discounting units common to many films (the study's heredity statistic). Each twin pair gets up to three likeness-matched remake pairs. Null: mismatched same-genre, same-decade pairs.
ideas.rivals: Rare shared words and named details, TF-IDF cosine, mean-pooled hidden state, random units, and an LLM asked 'remake or coincidence?', scored only where it cannot name either film, as it may remember them. Sentence-embedding similarity is neutralised by the matching. Rare shared words are most dangerous: remakes keep odd details as words. If they win, descent is readable without neurons.
ideas.premise: P1. A meme must be copied, not merely present. A pass shows units carry lineage information that similarity lacks. If rare words do as well, P1 gains nothing. If every method fails, Wikipedia plots cannot support the study's influence claims at all.
ideas.bio: Homology against convergent evolution; neutral markers such as shared pseudogenes.
ideas.cost: S to M. About 900 plots, minutes of forward passes. Cleaning the twin list, matching pairs and fetching translated plots is the work: three to four days.
ideas.payoff: A way to say 'this was copied' instead of 'this is similar', the gap in every influence claim so far. Also a reusable labelled set of descent and convergence pairs.
ideas.risk: Twin films are often not independent: studios race from leaked scripts, so some 'coincidences' are copies. Remakes resemble their originals far more than twins resemble each other, so matching on likeness may leave too few pairs.
ideas.review: Counted the list: 149 rows, about 110 after a keyword screen for shared sources, not 150. Added cross-language plots against copied wording, a named matching measure and a memory guard for the LLM judge. Remaining weakness: about 90 twin pairs can resolve only a 0.10 neuron-over-word gap.

ideas.title: Lindy effect: does a meme's age forecast survival?
ideas.question: Among story memes alive in films at a cut-off year, does age predict how well each holds its share over the next 20 years, beyond current frequency and random copying?
ideas.hypothesis: Each doubling of a meme's age at the 1992 cut-off raises its 1993 to 2012 retention (later share of films divided by its 1973 to 1992 share) by at least 5%, controlling that earlier share and its trend, and the effect exceeds 95% of 1,000 random-copying simulations.
ideas.falsifier: The age effect's 95% interval lies below 2% per doubling, or inside the random-copying range, for every unit type: Lindy is frequency in disguise. For neurons: the neuron age effect is no larger than the effect for TF-IDF terms or trope tags (difference interval includes zero). About 300 unit clusters give power 0.94 for a partial correlation of 0.2.
ideas.data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus: 42,306 Wikipedia film plots, 39,589 with a release year (counted 2026-11-08), CC BY-SA; 7,951 fall in 1973 to 1992 and 19,791 in 1993 to 2012. About 1,300 predate 1930, so ages are capped near 60 years. Series links from Wikidata (CC0). Trope tags from Gala et al. 2020 (licence unconfirmed; commit IDs only). Names masked.
ideas.method: Units: neuron families chosen on a random third of films from all years, scored on the rest. Age: years since a unit first passed 0.5% of films, capped for units already common in the 1930s. Regression across unit clusters, with bootstrap intervals. Null: random copying (each film draws memes from earlier films by frequency), with real yearly counts.
ideas.rivals: The same analysis with TF-IDF terms, TV Tropes tags, sentence-embedding clusters, LLM-listed traits and random non-meme units; current frequency alone. Frequency alone is most dangerous: under random copying old memes are simply the common ones. Trope tags may show Lindy with no model, which still settles the conjecture.
ideas.premise: Assumes both. Lindy found equally in words and tropes is a fact about culture that needs no neurons. A stronger age effect for neuron units than for words, in both Qwen and Llama, would support P1 (ideas outlive their wording) and P2.
ideas.bio: Taxon age against extinction risk; Van Valen's constant-extinction law is the null.
ideas.cost: S to M. About 6 hours of forward passes per model at the rate in preregistration/sources/neuron_timing_qwen3-8b.json (optimistic); store presence bits only. Simulations take minutes.
ideas.payoff: The first measured test of 'old ideas are the safe ones' against the right null. If it holds, age is a free forecasting feature; if not, Lindy is survivorship bias.
ideas.risk: Wikipedia remembers the old films that still matter, so a meme that lived only in forgotten early films is dated too young and looks short-lived: survivorship can fake Lindy. Summaries were all written after 2001 in modern words, so wording drift, the neurons' best case, is absent.
ideas.review: Units were chosen on pre-1973 films, which excluded every young meme; now chosen on a random third. Thin pre-1930 coverage caps ages, now stated. Swapped an unreachable trope table for Gala et al. Remaining weakness: Wikipedia's memory of old films can fake the effect.

ideas.title: Memeplexes: are memes gained and lost together?
ideas.question: Along documented adaptation links, are memes of the same bundle kept or dropped together more often than their everyday co-occurrence and the link's overall fidelity predict?
ideas.hypothesis: For unit pairs in one bundle (bundles defined on unrelated films), the odds of being kept or dropped together across about 2,000 source-to-adaptation links are at least 1.5 times the odds across matched unlinked film pairs, and the excess holds in at least 10 unrelated source lineages.
ideas.falsifier: The ratio's 95% interval lies below 1.2: bundles travel together no more than their everyday co-occurrence predicts. For neurons: neuron bundles show no higher co-change odds than word-topic bundles or TV Tropes co-occurrence bundles (difference interval includes zero). Power depends on how many bundle pairs each of the 2,000 links carries; count that on development films first.
ideas.data: Wikidata 'based on' and 'derivative work' links (99,206 and 40,376 statements, CC0; 15,706 'based on' links start from a film) where both works have a Wikipedia plot (CC BY-SA): sample 2,000 links from at least 500 sources, plus 2,000 matched unlinked pairs. Bundles learned on CMU Movie Summary Corpus films outside those lineages. Names masked.
ideas.method: Units: neuron families, no two tracking one word. Bundle: units that co-occur in development films, each appearing without the others in at least 20% of cases, and peaking in different sentences (so not one scene). Statistic: joint loss and joint gain along links against unlinked pairs matched on genre, decade and likeness. Second null: shuffle keeping row and column totals.
ideas.rivals: Bundles from a topic model on the same masked text, from TV Tropes tag co-occurrence, from LLM-listed traits, and from random frequency-matched unit sets; summary length. The topic model is most dangerous: a scene's vocabulary travels together. Then bundles are real but are scenes, and neurons add nothing.
ideas.premise: P1. Memeplex is a core term of memetics that has never been measured. Co-change beyond everyday co-occurrence, repeated across lineages, gives the unit a heredity property a concept detector lacks. If word topics do as well, bundling belongs to text, not neurons.
ideas.bio: Linkage disequilibrium and supergenes; Pagel's test for correlated trait change.
ideas.cost: M. About 8,000 plots plus development films: a few hours of forward passes. Name masking, matching unlinked pairs and cleaning the links take most of a week.
ideas.payoff: The first measured memeplexes: a list of bundles that travel as wholes and the lineages they travelled in. Tells an adapter which elements can be dropped alone and which come as a set.
ideas.risk: Co-change may still reflect settings: drop the courtroom and every courtroom unit goes. Wikipedia summaries of adaptations are sometimes written from the source's summary, inflating retention; a plot from another-language Wikipedia for one end (Tell Me Again) is the check.
ideas.review: Units that co-occur will also seem to change together between any two films, so the shuffle null was too easy. Added matched unlinked pairs as the comparison and a different-sentence rule against one-scene bundles. Remaining weakness: adaptation summaries may be written from the source's summary.
sources: Wikidata (based on P144, derivative work P4969)

ideas.title: Thirty-year return: do faded memes come back?
ideas.question: After a story meme peaks in films and fades, does its share rebound about 30 years later more than at other lags, and is the rebound carried by directors who were young at the peak?
ideas.hypothesis: For memes whose share peaked between 1930 and 1965 and then halved, share 25 to 35 years after the peak is at least 10% higher than the mean of the flanking lags (10 to 20 and 40 to 45 years), in at least three peak decades, and beats 95% of simulations where films copy earlier films' memes by frequency alone.
ideas.falsifier: The rebound's 95% interval lies below 3%, or inside the simulated range, for every unit type: no 30-year return in film plots. For neurons: the neuron rebound does not exceed the rebound for TF-IDF terms or trope tags (difference interval includes zero). About 200 unit clusters should put a 10% rebound at three standard errors or more (rough estimate).
ideas.data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus: 39,589 dated Wikipedia film plots, CC BY-SA; 8,373 fall in 1930 to 1965, about 230 a year, so shares use five-year bins. Director birth dates from Wikidata (CC0): 19,200 of a non-random 20,000-film sample had one (2026-11-08). Remake lags from Wikidata 'based on' links (1,499 film-to-film) as a text-free check.
ideas.method: Units chosen on a random third of films; series built on the rest. Fade: a five-year peak at least 1.5 times the unit's median share, then 10 years below it. Return curve: mean share at each lag. Null: random copying with real yearly counts. Secondary: is the rebound larger in films by directors aged 5 to 25 at the peak?
ideas.rivals: The same return curve from TF-IDF terms, trope tags and genre labels; the histogram of remake lags, which needs no text, against a null that respects how many films existed each year; random units. TF-IDF is most dangerous: revivals reuse period words. If remake lags alone show the 30-year peak, no unit is needed.
ideas.premise: Assumes both. Mostly a test of the conjecture. P1 gains only if neuron units show a rebound among name-masked plots where word units show none; P2 only if Qwen and Llama give the same return curve. A known rival view: retellings prefer young sources (Karsdorp and van den Bosch 2016).
ideas.bio: Seed banks releasing dormant variants; sensitive-period imprinting.
ideas.cost: S to M. Reuses the corpus pass (about 6 hours per model). Series and simulations take minutes; the Wikidata join for the secondary takes a day.
ideas.payoff: A number for when a faded meme comes back, which Mike wanted for timing a revival, or evidence that the 30-year cycle is folklore. If the secondary holds, a forecast rule: watch what peaked when today's 45-year-old creators were 15.
ideas.risk: One shared cause can fake a cycle: war memes peak in the 1940s and return with 1970s war films. Hence the three-decades rule, but only about four peak decades exist. Wikipedia's coverage of old films favours those later revived or remade.
ideas.review: The draft tested a mechanism (directors' youth) before showing any return exists, and period settings confounded it. Rewrote as a direct return-lag test with the director test as a secondary; the mechanism is kept as a seed. Remaining weakness: few independent peak decades, and Wikipedia favours revived films.

ideas.title: Remix ledger: new memes or new combinations?
ideas.question: Over a century of films, does novelty arrive as new units or as first-time pairings of old units, once the measurement is checked on remixes with known recipes?
ideas.hypothesis: Check: on 300 synthetic remixes the ledger ranks the true sources above matched decoys and its inherited shares correlate at least 0.6 with the planted shares. Then, in films after 1980, the share of units that were rare before exceeds the date-shuffled baseline by under 2 percentage points, while the new-pair share exceeds it by at least 5.
ideas.falsifier: Check correlation below 0.4 for neurons, or not above the best rival by 0.1: the ledger cannot be trusted (300 remixes separate 0.6 from 0.4 by over four standard errors). Conjecture: a post-1980 excess of rare-before units of 5 points or more means real novelty beyond recombination.
ideas.data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (39,589 dated plots, 25,208 after 1980, CC BY-SA), names masked. 300 synthetic remixes written by a small open model from two to four known source plots in set proportions, reworded by a second model; released CC BY-SA. Paired summaries of one story (Tell Me Again: 96,831 summaries, 29,505 stories, CC BY-SA 4.0) set the noise floor.
ideas.method: Units chosen on a random third of films from all years. For each other film, in release order: the share of its units that were rare before (in under 0.5% of earlier films) and the share of its unit pairs never seen together. Baseline: the same ledger with release dates shuffled within genre, which removes a fixed list's saturation.
ideas.rivals: The same ledger with word n-grams, TV Tropes or keyword pairs (Sreenivasan's method), embedding nearest-neighbour distance, and an LLM asked to list each film's sources. Keyword pairs are most dangerous: human-named and model-free. The check on synthetic remixes says which ledger to believe, so a rival's win still answers the conjecture.
ideas.premise: P1. A model's units are a closed list, so the ledger registers only novelty the model has a unit for; training after every film in the corpus helps here. Failing the check exposes that limit. Passing it ahead of keyword pairs would support P1 as a way to measure originality.
ideas.bio: Recombination against new mutation; exon shuffling against de novo genes.
ideas.cost: M. About 6 hours of forward passes per model for the corpus, a day of local generation for the remixes, a week in all.
ideas.payoff: 'Everything is a remix' turned into three measured shares per work (inherited, new, newly combined) with a known error. An originality score that can be audited.
ideas.risk: 'New' units may be new things in the world (phones, wars) more than new story ideas, and words catch those equally. Wikipedia covers few early films, so early works look more original than they were. LLM-written remixes may be easier to unpick than human ones.
ideas.review: Units chosen on pre-1950 films could never be new, and a fixed list is all seen within a few hundred films, so the hypothesis passed by construction. Units now come from all years and 'new' means rare before. Remix licence corrected to share-alike. Remaining weakness: the closed unit list.
sources: Ferguson, Everything is a Remix (video series)

ideas.title: Do acclaimed creators borrow from more sources?
ideas.question: Do directors whose films draw on a wider spread of earlier works earn more critical recognition, and within one director's career are the recognised films the broader ones?
ideas.hypothesis: Within a director's films, one standard deviation more source breadth (the effective number of distinct genre-and-decade groups among a film's 20 closest earlier sources) raises the odds of an award nomination by at least 10%, with summary length and release year controlled. Between directors, mean breadth predicts nominations in the same direction.
ideas.falsifier: The within-director effect's 95% interval lies below 3% per standard deviation, or is negative, for every unit type: the hunch fails. For neurons: neuron breadth adds no held-out likelihood over breadth from trope tags and embeddings (interval includes zero). If the declared-source gate fails, the test is not run.
ideas.data: CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia plots, CC BY-SA), summaries cut to one length band. Directors, nominations and awards from Wikidata (P57, P1411, P166; CC0): 6,950 films with a Freebase ID carry a nomination (counted 2026-11-08). Expect about 3,000 directors with four or more films, where a 10% effect is roughly three standard errors (an estimate); count before registering.
ideas.method: Sources: earlier films ranked by inheritance of a film's rare units (the study's heredity statistic), own films excluded. Gate: where Wikidata declares a source (P144, P941), the ranking must put it in the top 20 at least 20% of the time (chance: about 0.1%). Breadth: effective number of groups in the top 20. Null: breadth shuffled among each director's films.
ideas.rivals: Breadth from TF-IDF neighbours, sentence-embedding neighbours, the mean-pooled hidden state, TV Tropes tags, the count of declared Wikidata sources, an LLM asked how many sources a plot draws on, the film's own genre count and summary length. Genre count is most dangerous: breadth may only mean 'a film that mixes genres'.
ideas.premise: Assumes both. Resemblance is not influence, so this tests a correlate of the hunch. P1 gains only if neuron breadth predicts acclaim after tag and embedding breadth are in the model and the declared-source gate passes.
ideas.bio: Hybrid vigour; gene flow from many source populations.
ideas.cost: M. Reuses the corpus pass (about 6 hours per model); a week for the Wikidata join and the declared-source gate.
ideas.payoff: Evidence for or against advice given to every creative team: read widely, borrow widely. A per-creator breadth profile that can be checked against declared influences.
ideas.risk: Awards track fame, budget and prestige genres, and Wikidata records them unevenly. Famous films have longer, richer summaries, which can fake breadth even after trimming. A 10% effect sits near the detection limit.
ideas.review: Sources came from the method itself, and famous films have longer summaries, which fakes breadth. Added a numeric declared-source gate, equal-length summaries and a within-director comparison that holds fame fixed. Remaining weakness: resemblance is not borrowing, and Wikidata awards are patchy and fame-driven.
sources: Wikipedia: List of Bob Dylan songs based on earlier tunes
Wikidata (nominated for P1411, award received P166)

ideas.title: Obscure sources win acclaim, familiar sources win revenue
ideas.question: Do films whose closest earlier sources are little known earn critical recognition, while films with well-known sources earn box office?
ideas.note: From the originality grid in Mike's earlier notes (obscure or familiar source, conscious or not). CMU plots (7,531 with box office), Wikidata awards; source fame from Wikipedia pageviews, which measure fame today, not at release. Rival: embedding nearest ancestors. Shares CJ27's pipeline and its declared-source gate.

ideas.title: Does a bundle protect its members in retelling?
ideas.question: In LLM retelling chains, do the remaining parts of a meme bundle decay faster when one part has been removed from the seed story?
ideas.note: The causal half of the memeplex claim ('none would be remembered alone'). Truth by construction, after Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023. Rivals: keyword and LLM-judge detection of the parts. Laptop, small open models; follows CJ24. LLM retellers are not human audiences.

ideas.title: Fidelity, fecundity, longevity in folktales
ideas.question: Do tale types whose tellings vary least in meme profile occur in more populations and reconstruct as older?
ideas.note: Dawkins's three replicator traits. ATU-labelled Folktexts (Zenodo 6575263) against the da Silva and Tehrani 2016 matrix of 275 types by 50 populations. Rival: lexical variance across tellings. The overlap may be under 100 types, so power is the worry.

ideas.title: Meme fatigue in headline frames
ideas.question: Does the click lift of a winning headline frame shrink with how often that frame ran in the previous 4 to 6 weeks?
ideas.note: The ad-fatigue rule of thumb, on Upworthy's dated randomised tests; frames chosen on the exploratory split. Rival: regular expressions and n-gram counts, which should win on literal templates. Biology: negative frequency-dependent selection. Complements CJ21.

ideas.title: Concept beats variant
ideas.question: Does the distance between two headline arms predict the size of their click gap, so that bigger creative changes give bigger differences?
ideas.note: From the concept, theme, variant testing framework the notes credit to Seufert. Upworthy arm pairs; model true-effect variance against distance, net of sampling noise. Rivals: edit distance, TF-IDF, embeddings. Upworthy fixes the story, so only variant-level distance is testable.

ideas.title: Do rivals converge?
ideas.question: Does the distance between competing firms' descriptions of themselves shrink year on year, as 'memetic convergence' claims?
ideas.note: Candidate dated public text: annual-report business sections on SEC EDGAR (not checked this session). Rivals: TF-IDF cosine and Mike's tag-count distance, likely winners because firms repeat words. Register as an expected loss that marks the method's boundary.

ideas.title: Mike's three declared families, words forced apart
ideas.question: Are the 15 works in the three story families named in Mike's 2022 talk deck recoverable against matched decoys when shared vocabulary is banned?
ideas.note: An author-declared test set that pre-dates the study. Paraphrase under a banned-word list built from TF-IDF top terms. Rivals: embeddings and an LLM asked which works belong together. Fifteen works is small; treat as a pilot.

ideas.title: Lindy across space
ideas.question: Does a work's success in a second language market forecast spread to many more, beyond its first-market success?
ideas.note: From the notes' claim that Lindy 'works across space as well as time'. Needs dated translation records; Wikidata language-edition and translation data are a candidate, not checked. Rival: metadata alone (editions so far). Neurons matter only for which memes travel.

ideas.title: Do creators replay their youth?
ideas.question: Among films of the same year and genre, does a film resemble the films released when its director was aged 5 to 25 more than other past films?
ideas.note: The mechanism moved out of CJ25; run only if CJ25 finds a return. CMU plots; Wikidata birth dates (19,200 of 20,000 films in a non-random sample had one). Exclude the roughly 2,100 plots tagged period, costume or historical, whose setting words fake the effect. Rival: TF-IDF era similarity. After Holbrook and Schindler 1989.

ideas.title: Who or what: sharer against content
ideas.question: With the content held fixed, how much of a post's success do its words explain, compared with who posted it, where and when?
ideas.note: From the notes' point, after Girard, that the sharer often matters more than the meme. Reddit resubmissions (SNAP: 132,308 posts of repeated images; Lakkaraju et al. 2013). Rival: title n-grams. Martin et al. 2016 put content under 0.05 of variance on Twitter. A low ceiling limits any content-only memetics.

ideas.title: Are there only so many plots?
ideas.question: As films are added, does the count of distinct plot-level clusters level off, as 'seven plots' and 'six arcs' claim?
ideas.note: CMU plots, names masked. A species-accumulation curve with a richness estimate. Cluster films, not units: a fixed unit list levels off by construction. Rivals: word-sentiment arcs (Reagan et al. 2016) and embedding clusters. Wikipedia's summary style may impose the sameness.
